articles.summary: The maritime war between Russia and Ukraine has expanded far beyond the Black Sea, with a Russian naval corvette sunk in Libya and a sanctioned Russian cargo ship attacked in the Baltic over the weekend. articles.body: Africa Containers Europe Operations Ports and Logistics Tankers No safe harbour as maritime war spreads beyond Black Sea Sam Chambers November 23, 2026 0 378 1 minute read X.com X.com The maritime war between Russia and Ukraine has expanded far beyond the Black Sea, with a Russian naval corvette sunk in Libya and a sanctioned Russian cargo ship attacked in the Baltic over the weekend. The Russian navy’s Merkury, a Project 20380 corvette, was struck at the port of Benghazi on Sunday (pictured) while taking on fuel and supplies. Officials from Libya’s eastern administration said suspected sea drones attacked the vessel, sparking a fire. Satellite imagery subsequently showed the warship capsized and largely submerged alongside the quay. Two Libyan military officials told the Associated Press that six Ukrainian sea drones had been launched from western Libya, with four intercepted and two hitting the warship. A second attack was reported off Benghazi later on Sunday, with explosive-laden sea drones striking a Maltese-flagged merchant vessel (see video below). Libyan authorities said the crew had been rescued, with some receiving treatment for minor injuries. The Mediterranean strikes came just 24 hours after the Russian-flagged Sparta II, a US-sanctioned cargo ship operated by Oboronlogistika, which provides logistics services to Russia’s defence ministry, was attacked in the Gulf of Finland. The 121 m vessel was sailing from St Petersburg to Kaliningrad when two drones struck in international waters on Saturday, setting the ship ablaze. All 16 crewmembers were evacuated as the burning vessel drifted into Finnish territorial waters. Finnish, Estonian and Russian rescue assets battled the blaze throughout the weekend before the Russian rescue vessel Murman began towing the damaged ship back towards Russian waters on Sunday. Finnish authorities reported no pollution, although the vessel had developed a slight list. Meanwhile, Russia’s defence ministry claimed on Sunday that its forces had struck a dry cargo vessel carrying dual-use goods northeast of Odesa, along with port infrastructure at Kiliya on the Ukrainian Danube. The maritime attacks coincided with continuing strikes against energy infrastructure. Early on Monday, Ukrainian monitoring channels reported a major fire at Russia’s Novoshakhtinsk refinery in the Rostov region following a drone attack. The extent of the damage remains unclear. On Friday, Ukraine’s military confirmed that an earlier strike on the Kaleykino oil pumping station in Tatarstan, a key hub feeding the Druzhba pipeline, had damaged three large storage tanks. articles.body: Asia Shipyards ASL Marine exits Batam shipyard in $23m deal Adis Ajdin November 23, 2026 0 12 1 minute read Cemara Intan Shipyard Cemara Intan Shipyard Singapore-listed ASL Marine Holdings is selling an underused shipyard in Indonesia for IDR420bn ($23m), in a deal expected to generate a gain of around S$17.2m ($13.3m) before taxes and transaction expenses. The marine group disclosed that its wholly owned subsidiary, Intan Overseas Investments, has signed a sale and purchase agreement with Indonesian shipping company PT Global Sinergi Maritim to dispose of its entire stake in PT Cemara Intan Shipyard. The Batam-based business, incorporated in 2006, is involved in shipbuilding, repair and general engineering.ASL said the yard’s limited operational activity had prompted the decision to sell, allowing the group to concentrate resources on its remaining businesses. The IDR420bn consideration, equivalent to approximately S$29.8m, includes settlement of the shipyard subsidiary’s obligations to creditors. The transaction remains subject to conditions, with completion to be announced separately. Cemara Intan had net tangible assets of S$12.6m at the end of June and recorded a S$1.6m loss for ASL’s 2026 financial year. The Singapore group said it plans to use the disposal proceeds for capital expenditure and working capital. ASL retains shipbuilding and repair operations in Singapore and Indonesia, alongside a chartering fleet of more than 180 tugboats and barges. Its remaining shipyard activities cover vessels ranging from tugs and tankers to specialised offshore tonnage. articles.body: Asia Middle East Shipyards Tankers Gulf Energy Maritime doubles down on LR1s in South Korea Adis Ajdin November 23, 2026 0 32 1 minute read K Shipbuilding K Shipbuilding Dubai-based tanker owner Gulf Energy Maritime (GEM) has signed up for another series of LR1 product tanker newbuildings at South Korea’s K Shipbuilding, extending its investment in the panamax segment. Shipbuilding sources have identified GEM as the Middle Eastern customer behind a package of up to four 74,000 dwt vessels at the Jinhae-based yard, with delivery slots reportedly lined up for 2029. The potential four-ship deal has been valued by market sources at around $264m, putting the price at about $66m per vessel. K Shipbuilding announced the contracts earlier this year without naming the buyers. Its original disclosure covered two firm LR1 vessels and options for another two, alongside a separate order for two 50,000 dwt MR tankers from a European customer. The newbuildings will meet IMO’s EEDI Phase III requirements and feature designs allowing conversion to LNG or methanol propulsion. The deal marks another round of contracting between GEM and K Shipbuilding. The Dubai owner was previously linked to four 75,000 dwt LR1 tankers at the same yard in July 2024 . GEM has also been expanding its MR fleet. Earlier this year, the company ordered six 50,000 dwt product tankers at HD Hyundai’s South Korean and Vietnamese facilities in a deal worth around $300m. The company’s website currently lists 18 vessels in its operating fleet, including five LR1s, along with another 10 ships on order. articles.title: COP31 collapse casts shadow over shipping’s net-zero showdown
articles.summary: Global climate negotiations have collapsed in Turkey just as shipping’s fiercely contested decarbonisation talks resume at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) in London. The COP31 summit in Antalya ended on Sunday without an overarching agreement after nearly 200 countries failed to bridge divisions over...
articles.body: Environment Regulatory COP31 collapse casts shadow over shipping’s net-zero showdown Sam Chambers November 23, 2026 0 38 2 minutes read Piet Sinke / Maasmond Maritime Piet Sinke / Maasmond Maritime Global climate negotiations have collapsed in Turkey just as shipping’s fiercely contested decarbonisation talks resume at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) in London. The COP31 summit in Antalya ended on Sunday without an overarching agreement after nearly 200 countries failed to bridge divisions over fossil fuels and climate finance. The European Union, Britain and vulnerable island states rejected a proposed Antalya Pact that made no explicit reference to moving away from coal, oil and gas, while Saudi Arabia and Russia resisted tougher language. Some subsidiary decisions were agreed, but the summit’s central political declaration failed. The acrimonious outcome provides a troubling backdrop for IMO delegates, who begin five days of technical discussions today ahead of next week’s Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC 85). Shipping’s proposed Net-Zero Framework, approved in draft form last year but not adopted, combines tightening greenhouse gas fuel-intensity requirements with financial compliance payments and incentives for cleaner fuels. While delegates have made headway on technical standards, the economic element remains deeply divisive. The US opposes mandatory emissions charges, while other governments are pressing for changes to targets, payment structures and the distribution of funds. Adoption was postponed in October 2025, and an extraordinary IMO meeting is provisionally scheduled for December 4, subject to confirmation at MEPC 85. The similarities with Antalya are striking: who pays for decarbonisation, how quickly fossil fuels should be displaced and how developing economies are supported. Last week, nine shipping associations, including Cruise Lines International Association (CLIA), BIMCO, the International Chamber of Shipping, Intertanko and the World Shipping Council, urged governments to agree practical and enforceable global rules, warning that prolonged uncertainty threatens investment in alternative-fuel ships and fuel supply. Unlike COP’s consensus-driven negotiations, IMO treaty amendments can be adopted by a two-thirds majority of parties present and voting. That offers a procedural route forward, but no guarantee of agreement. For shipowners already navigating the EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime, the stakes include the risk of overlapping regional rules if global talks fail again. Although COP31 failed to produce an overarching deal, shipping left Antalya with voluntary commitments rather than new binding rules. More than 30 organisations backed a target for electricity to supply at least 20% of international shipping’s final energy demand by 2035. Guinea, Côte d’Ivoire and Mauritania signed agreements to develop carbon-financing systems potentially covering shipping, without setting levy dates. A separate coalition endorsed so-called blue shipping corridors combining cleaner fuels with marine conservation. Guo Yang, general manager of the company’s second business department, has voluntarily surrendered to authorities and is undergoing disciplinary and supervisory investigations, according to a notice issued by Shanghai’s disciplinary inspection authorities. The investigation is being conducted by the disciplinary inspection team stationed at China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), together with the supervisory commission of Shanghai’s Chongming district. Established in 2012 and listed in Hong Kong in 2019, the company provides financial and operating leases to shipowners and operators worldwide. The company’s fleet stood at 135 vessels at the end of 2025, including 114 operating ships and 21 vessels under construction. articles.title: Singapore Shipping returns to newbuilds with $210m car carrier deal
articles.summary: Singapore Shipping Corporation (SSC) has returned to the newbuilding market with a $210m investment in two LNG dual-fuel car carriers in China, launching a fleet renewal programme that could eventually reach $400m. The Singapore-listed owner has signed contracts with Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI) and China...
articles.body: Asia Operations Singapore Shipping returns to newbuilds with $210m car carrier deal Adis Ajdin November 23, 2026 0 58 1 minute read Singapore Shipping Corp Singapore Shipping Corp Singapore Shipping Corporation (SSC) has returned to the newbuilding market with a $210m investment in two LNG dual-fuel car carriers in China, launching a fleet renewal programme that could eventually reach $400m. The Singapore-listed owner has signed contracts with Guangzhou Shipyard International (GSI) and China Shipbuilding Trading Company (CSTC) for two 7,000 ceu pure car and truck carriers (PCTCs). The ships are scheduled for delivery in March and June 2031, respectively. According to the company’s stock exchange filing, the shipbuilding contracts carry a combined price of $187m, or $93.5m per vessel. The total estimated investment rises to $210m when financing costs, stores, spares and other expenses are included. The deal marks SSC’s first newbuilding move in more than a decade and comes with much of its existing car carrier fleet approaching retirement. The company currently owns five PCTCs with a combined capacity of 32,410 ceu. Four were built between 1999 and 2004, while its youngest vessel dates from 2015. SSC warned in its latest annual report that around 80% of its vessels are approaching the end of their economic useful lives, requiring substantial investment in replacement tonnage. The two contracted ships could be followed by further orders. SSC has sought regulatory clearance for potential acquisitions of up to four PCTCs at a combined cost of as much as $400m. The Singapore Exchange has granted a conditional waiver from shareholder approval requirements for the programme. However, one condition remained outstanding at the time of the announcement, with SSC holding voting undertakings from shareholders representing 49.42% against the required level of more than 50%. Executive chairman C K Ow said the investment is part of a long-term renewal strategy rather than a bet on current car carrier market conditions. SSC, whose business also includes shipmanagement, shipping agency, terminal operations and logistics, plans to finance the newbuildings through existing cash resources and external funding. articles.title: Gulftainer signs 10-year partnership with CU Lines for Khorfakkan Port
articles.summary: Gulftainer has entered into a 10-year strategic partnership with China United Lines (CU Lines), securing long-term container volumes through Khorfakkan Port in the United Arab Emirates. The agreement aims to strengthen trade connections between China and the UAE while supporting more reliable cargo flows through the...
articles.body: Gulftainer has entered into a 10-year strategic partnership with China United Lines (CU Lines), securing long-term container volumes through Khorfakkan Port in the United Arab Emirates. The agreement aims to strengthen trade connections between China and the UAE while supporting more reliable cargo flows through the port. According to Gulftainer, the partnership will also connect maritime services with inland dry ports and logistics facilities in Sharjah, offering customers a more integrated transport network. The arrangement builds on existing cooperation between the two companies. Earlier in November, Gulftainer’s container shipping division, GT Lines, announced cooperation with CU Lines on the CGX service, also identified as KCX 5. The service connects Qingdao, Ningbo, Shekou and Nansha in China with Port Klang in Malaysia and Khorfakkan in the UAE. Long-term agreement strengthens Khorfakkan’s role The new partnership provides a longer-term framework for cargo movements through Khorfakkan, supporting Gulftainer’s efforts to develop the port as a gateway for trade between Asia and the Gulf. It also forms part of the company’s wider strategy to integrate port operations with inland container handling and logistics services in Sharjah. Gulftainer said the agreement is intended to provide customers with greater reliability and long-term capacity. The company has not disclosed the container volumes covered by the partnership or its financial terms. Further operational details, including any additional service commitments under the 10-year arrangement, have not been announced.

articles.summary: French authorities are preparing a difficult salvage operation to free a 28,200 dwt bulk carrier driven onto an Atlantic beach during a storm, with failed generators and shallow water hampering efforts to pull it clear. The 2011-built, Malta-flagged Miro G grounded early on Friday at Cap de l’Homy, near Lit-et-Mixe...
articles.body: Dry Cargo Europe Operations Grounded bulker faces complex salvage operation off French coast Sam Chambers November 23, 2026 0 373 1 minute read French Navy French Navy French authorities are preparing a difficult salvage operation to free a 28,200 dwt bulk carrier driven onto an Atlantic beach during a storm, with failed generators and shallow water hampering efforts to pull it clear. The 2011-built, Malta-flagged Miro G grounded early on Friday at Cap de l’Homy, near Lit-et-Mixe in southwestern France, after gusts of 48 knots dragged its anchors. The vessel was sailing in ballast from Santander to Rouen when it encountered difficulties. French air force helicopters evacuated 19 of the vessel’s 22 seafarers on Friday. The master and two crew remained to assist recovery teams but were airlifted out on Saturday alongside eight salvors, experts and an insurance representative as weather deteriorated. French maritime authorities stabilised the ship by taking on ballast water, but that water must now be pumped out to lighten the hull for refloating. Both main generators are unavailable, leaving teams working to restore temporary electrical power. Les Abeilles International’s rescue tug Abeille Bretagne, dispatched from Brest, will have to operate at least 900 m offshore because of shallow water. Passing a 1,000 m Kevlar towline to the grounded bulker, which is lying parallel to the beach, presents another major challenge. Authorities have warned that the operation’s outcome remains highly uncertain, with declining tidal heights narrowing the window for a successful pull. A 1,000 m exclusion zone has been established. Although the ship was sailing without cargo, it has around 100 tonnes of fuel aboard. French naval surveillance has detected no pollution. articles.title: Spain joins growing global crackdown on scrubbers
articles.summary: Spain has become the latest country to clamp down on ship scrubbers, announcing a nationwide ban on washwater discharges in ports and designated coastal waters from July 1, 2027. Unlike countries that have initially targeted open-loop systems, Spain’s new royal decree covers open-loop, closed-loop and hybrid...
articles.body: Environment Europe Regulatory Spain joins growing global crackdown on scrubbers Sam Chambers November 23, 2026 0 138 1 minute read Spain has become the latest country to clamp down on ship scrubbers, announcing a nationwide ban on washwater discharges in ports and designated coastal waters from July 1, 2027. Unlike countries that have initially targeted open-loop systems, Spain’s new royal decree covers open-loop, closed-loop and hybrid scrubbers from day one. The restrictions apply to all merchant vessels, regardless of flag, operating in Spanish internal maritime waters, port areas and designated anchorages within territorial waters. Ships will not have to remove their scrubbers but must switch to compliant low-sulphur fuel or retain wastewater onboard for subsequent disposal ashore. Spain’s decision goes beyond last year’s OSPAR agreement, which requires northeast Atlantic countries to ban open-loop discharges in ports and internal waters by July 2027, extending to all scrubber types in 2029. Madrid is bringing forward the latter deadline by two years and extending the restrictions to Mediterranean ports. Spanish shipowners’ association Anave welcomed regulatory consistency but questioned the absence of a published environmental risk assessment justifying the accelerated timetable. It also raised concerns about whether ports will have sufficient waste reception capacity. The decision follows similar moves elsewhere. Denmark, Sweden and Finland banned open-loop discharges in their territorial waters in July 2025, with restrictions on closed-loop systems following in 2029. Greenland’s parliament voted last month to introduce a phased ban, starting in July 2027. China, Singapore and Turkey already enforce restrictions in their waters. Scrubbers have become increasingly controversial since the IMO’s global sulphur cap took effect in 2020. While the technology allows ships to continue burning cheaper high-sulphur fuel oil, environmental campaigners argue it transfers pollution from the atmosphere into the oceans. Spain says scrubber washwater can contain heavy metals and organic pollutants and contribute to marine acidification. articles.title: Tanker inferno greets UN oceans advocate’s swim through Hormuz
articles.summary: Three tankers have been hit by projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz in the space of 15 hours as more images emerge of the huge marine damage the nine-month war is having on the marine environment. The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC), in an update issued on Sunday, identified two of the vessels as the …
articles.body: Middle East Operations Tankers Tanker inferno greets UN oceans advocate’s swim through Hormuz Sam Chambers November 23, 2026 0 290 3 minutes read Lewis Pugh Foundation Lewis Pugh Foundation Three tankers have been hit by projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz in the space of 15 hours as more images emerge of the huge marine damage the nine-month war is having on the marine environment. The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC), in an update issued on Sunday, identified two of the vessels as the Hong Kong-flagged Torkel and Arina. Torkel was struck on its stern approximately 11 nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, early on Saturday, sparking a fire. The tanker was subsequently reported at anchor. Less than an hour later, Arina was hit in its engine room, 17 nautical miles east of Khasab. No casualties were reported in either incident, although the extent of the damage and any environmental impact remain unclear. A third tanker, whose identity has not been officially disclosed, was struck on its port bow eight nautical miles north of Khasab on Friday afternoon, also resulting in a fire. Iranian authorities claimed over the weekend that tankers had struck naval mines after entering restricted waters, but JMIC stressed that the claims remained unverified. The attacks bring the number of tankers struck in Hormuz since November 16 to seven. The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) centre also reported a separate incident on Sunday involving a tanker and military forces in the Gulf of Oman, off Iran’s southeastern coast. No details of the vessel or the forces involved were immediately available. JMIC continues to classify the threat in Hormuz as severe, warning that further attacks on tankers using the Omani side of the strait are highly likely. Lewis Pugh, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) patron of the oceans, has just completed a three-day, 15 km swim through the Strait of Hormuz, witnessing attacks on commercial shipping as he sought to draw international attention to the devastating environmental consequences of war. The swim took Pugh from Musandam Island in the Strait of Hormuz, to the Cape of Hormuz, at the northern tip of Oman’s Musandam Peninsula. On the first day of the swim, an oil tanker was struck by a projectile approximately four kilometres from where Pugh was swimming. He heard two explosions, followed by the sound of fighter jets overhead. The second day saw fireballs rising above a headland that separated Pugh from the burning LPG carrier, the Tara Gas (pictured above). On the return to port, he passed close to the vessel, which was still engulfed in flames. “My immediate thoughts were for the seafarers onboard,” said Pugh. “The flames were enormous. These vessels carry highly flammable gases, and an attack on one can have catastrophic consequences – not just for crewmembers, but also on the surrounding marine environment.” Throughout the three days, Pugh continued to hear explosions in the distance and fighter jets overhead. He also witnessed convoys of commercial vessels travelling close to the Omani coastline as they hurried to leave the Gulf, round the Musandam Peninsula and enter the Gulf of Oman. The Strait of Hormuz is far more than a vital shipping route. On one side are the dramatic mountains and fjords of Oman’s Musandam Peninsula. On the other are Iran’s remarkable mangrove forests. Beneath the surface lies a rich marine ecosystem, home to extraordinary wildlife, including dugongs, sea turtles and whale sharks. The environmental damage from the conflict is already severe. According to the United Nations, at least 175 vessels have been attacked since fighting began in late February. About 30 have caused significant pollution. Oil spills threaten marine wildlife and fragile habitats, including coral reefs, seagrass meadows and mangrove forests. More than a dozen Marine Protected Areas are reported to have been affected. Greenpeace has identified more than 600 possible oil spills across the Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Arabian Sea since the US-Iran war began on February 28, with satellite imagery showing a cumulative slick footprint of approximately 20,000 sq km. Not all detections have been conclusively linked to attacks on shipping. The environmental consequences could last for decades. A 2022 study published in the Journal of Marine Science and Engineering found extensive oil deposits along more than 25 km of Saudi Arabia’s Abu Ali Island coastline, almost 40 years after the 1983–85 Nowruz oil spills during the Iran-Iraq war. Researchers found oil contamination in 76% of 1,434 test pits, demonstrating how petroleum residues can persist long after surface slicks disappear. The danger goes far beyond oil pollution. Heavy metals and toxic chemicals can contaminate the sea for decades. Damage to desalination plants and energy infrastructure also threatens the fresh drinking water on which tens of millions of people across the Gulf depend. “When we look at the Strait of Hormuz, we see oil tankers, warships and a vital shipping route. But beneath the surface is an extraordinary natural world. It deserves our protection, not destruction,” said Pugh. A former maritime lawyer, endurance swimmer Pugh was appointed to his UN role in 2013. articles.title: CMA CGM shifts Manaus cargo from PEX2 to SEAS 2 service
articles.summary: CMA CGM has announced a new routing arrangement for container shipments between the Far East and Manaus, Brazil, shifting cargo from its PEX2 service to SEAS 2. Under the revised network, shipments will move through Rio de Janeiro before connecting with the weekly BRACO service operated by the group’s subsidiary,...
articles.body: CMA CGM has announced a new routing arrangement for container shipments between the Far East and Manaus, Brazil, shifting cargo from its PEX2 service to SEAS 2. Under the revised network, shipments will move through Rio de Janeiro before connecting with the weekly BRACO service operated by the group’s subsidiary, MERCOSUL. The change will establish a single routing arrangement managed by CMA CGM Group. According to the carrier, it is designed to improve service reliability and operational efficiency. SEAS 2 provides weekly connections with major export hubs across northern, central and southern China. Its first Brazilian call at Rio de Janeiro will serve as the transshipment point for Manaus cargo. New routing bypasses Panama Canal The BRACO service will provide weekly connections to and from Manaus, with a transit time of 11 days from Rio de Janeiro. The revised arrangement will also remove the need to route Manaus shipments through the Panama Canal. CMA CGM said the new structure will offer greater flexibility for cargo volumes while reducing exposure to operational constraints associated with the canal. The transition will take place across several scheduled sailings. The last PEX2 vessel carrying Manaus cargo will be CSCL LONG BEACH, voyage PEX0B0E19, which began its rotation at Vung Tau, Vietnam, on 18 November 2026. The final Manaus Shuttle sailing under the previous arrangement will be operated by CMA CGM ALEXANDRIA, voyage MAS0Y0S19, with arrival in Manaus expected on 20 January 2027. Meanwhile, COSCO SHIPPING BRAZIL, voyage SE2080W19, will be the first SEAS 2 vessel to carry Manaus cargo under the new arrangement. The vessel is scheduled to begin its rotation at Qingdao, China, on 4 December 2026. The changes form part of CMA CGM’s wider adjustments to its services connecting Asia with South America’s east coast.

articles.title: Going beyond visibility to being valued
articles.summary: Despite calls for change, much of maritime still has manels and treats inclusion as a separate box to tick. Maritime SheEO founder Sanjam Sahi Gupta explains why our industry still has a long way to go, and discusses the need to build spaces where inclusion is the foundation rather than an afterthought. Recent years...
articles.body: Asia Contributions Operations Going beyond visibility to being valued Splash November 23, 2026 0 222 4 minutes read Synergy Synergy Despite calls for change, much of maritime still has manels and treats inclusion as a separate box to tick. Maritime SheEO founder Sanjam Sahi Gupta explains why our industry still has a long way to go, and discusses the need to build spaces where inclusion is the foundation rather than an afterthought. Recent years have seen the maritime industry become fluent in the language of inclusion. But behind the language of inclusion, far too many are still slow to share power. The 2024 Women in Maritime survey tells us that women account for roughly 19% of the workforce among participating member states, and just 1% of seafarers. I can’t help wondering how many of those women will stay in an industry that is happy to count them but not always to empower them. We talk a great deal about recruiting more women. We talk far less about whether they are given real opportunities once they arrive. India tells both stories at once. The Directorate General of Shipping’s 2026 survey shows women seafarers rising from 0.77% of the seafarer workforce in 2019 to 2.17% in 2025. That is close to a threefold increase, and every woman behind that number deserves to be celebrated. Yet women officers accounted for only 0.1% of all seafarers in 2025. The pipeline is widening but it is not yet at the point of carrying women to where decisions are made. The same is true on shore. Women remain a minority in leadership and on conference stages. The all-male panel is still a mainstay of our industry calendar, and when women are invited to speak, they are too often asked to talk only about inclusion. Our women engineers, lawyers, financiers and seafarers have much more to say, yet few are given the chance to say it, or the room to falter, or even fail, while they learn. Even I, after a long career in maritime, am still sometimes spoken over, or invited simply to be counted rather than to have my opinion considered. It was with this in mind that we chose the theme for the recent 7th Maritime SheEO Conference in Mumbai: “She Owns. She Builds. She Invests.” For years, our industry has worked hard to get women through the door, and that work matters. The harder question is what happens next. Are women given visibility, a voice, meaningful responsibility and the ability to shape the decisions that matter? Or are they warmly welcomed into the room, then left without the authority to act? Leaders who made it count What gave me the most hope in Mumbai was watching leaders stand up and make public commitments. Capt Animesh Hore of Mitsui O.S.K. Lines (MOL) put the challenge plainly: once the door is open, do women receive real responsibility, authority and sponsorship? He asked every leader in the room to identify a talented woman, give her meaningful responsibility, and invest time, trust and influence in her. MOL backs it with its Human Capital 2035 targets: 20% women in Group Key Positions, 30% in Head Office management positions, and women making up 4% of total officers and engineers by 2030. Nathasha Egodage of Ceyline Group shared that a workforce survey found women made up 18% of the company, and announced Ceyline’s commitment to reach 30% by 2030. I admire that honesty. Publishing a baseline and setting a target is how accountability starts. Captain Deepak Correa announced that Fleet Management achieved a 30% increase in women seafarers by 2025, a result worth cheering. He also offered a wise warning. Good intentions are not enough, he said, and without effective implementation these efforts will fail. There must be ownership of the outcomes. Aditi Garg, group legal director at Fleet Management, explained that strong governance means creating an environment where people can contribute and challenge assumptions constructively. For Fleet, being “powered by people” means equal pay for equal work, women-specific PPE and medical provisions, well-being support and mentoring. She spoke with real pride about Captain Deepti Singh and Captain Nilam Pande, Fleet’s first and second women seafarers to reach the rank of master. I hope they will be the first of many. The Indian government is setting the tone too. Sameer Khare (Retd. IAS), chairman of the National Shipping Board, noted that India has moved from women’s development to women-led development. Section 4 of the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 requires at least four women among the nominated members of the National Shipping Board, which he called a legal commitment to representation at the apex of Indian shipping, not a symbolic one. Visibility is not power What connects these leaders is not sentiment but structure: targets that are published, outcomes that someone owns, and authority that is genuinely shared. That is the shift we need, from asking whether women are present to committing to the end result, and part of that result must be women who are empowered in their positions. Visibility alone cannot be our measure of success. A woman in the room is not always the same as a woman speaking with authority and expertise on a panel. Yet when an all-male panel takes place today, the explanation is still too often that no women speakers could be found. A photograph of a diverse team is not the same as a diverse board. If we count appearances rather than authority, we risk applauding progress that has not happened. That is why Maritime SheEO is growing. Our annual leadership conference remains our home for people and leadership, now joined by satellite events on technology and digitalisation, with a focus on women in STEM; ports, bunkering and freight forwarding; risk; and the ship lifecycle from building to recycling. Women belong in these conversations as experts, not as a separate agenda item. We haven’t moved beyond the need to drive inclusion, and we won’t wait for the manel to retire itself. Where there are too few forums for women experts to be heard, we will build them. I hope you will join us. articles.summary: The first cracks are showing in the tanker markets, as higher freight rates are now harder to absorb. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Gibson said that “refining margins have fallen sharply this month, led by gasoline. Asian gasoline cracks stand at just over $1/bbl, close to negative, the lowest in more than...
articles.body: Tanker Market: Lower Refining Margins Leaving Less Room to Pay for Freight in Hellenic Shipping News 23/11/2026 T he first cracks are showing in the tanker markets, as higher freight rates are now harder to absorb. In its latest weekly report, shipbroker Gibson said that “refining margins have fallen sharply this month, led by gasoline. Asian gasoline cracks stand at just over $1/bbl, close to negative, the lowest in more than three years and a stark drop when compared against more than $50/bbl at the start of October. Gasoil is holding up better but is well off its highs, Asian cracks are near $53/bbl, down from $87/bbl in mid-September, and European gasoil has dropped to $61/bbl. Refineries are still running hard to capture those margins, and gasoline, produced alongside regardless, is paying the price. Utilisation remains high, in the US for example, the thin autumn maintenance program we flagged in August (No Margin for Error) kept utilisation at 95.6% in October, against 90.6% in the previous two years”. According to Gibson, “these lower margins are leaving refiners less room to pay for freight, especially in the East. Record product cracks allowed record crude freight to be absorbed in September and October, but with margins now lower, that cost has to fall elsewhere. Freight has already taken part of the adjustment, with VLCC earnings from the Gulf to China around a quarter below their October peak, and sellers are bearing more of the remainder. Saudi Aramco has cut its December Arab Light price for Asia to a discount of $7/bbl, a six-year low, and Iraq is again offering Basrah crude at discounts of more than $30/bbl for loading inside the Gulf. If margins stay weak, freight may need to fall further to restore the balance, which could limit how far crude tanker rates can recover from the recent correction”. “Clean tanker rates outside the Gulf have moved decidedly lower. In the West, MRs from the US Gulf have dropped sharply, on a TCE basis now around $26,000/day, down around two thirds since late October. LR2s from the Mediterranean to the Far East (TC15) are at $60,000/day against $175,000/day in mid-October. In the East, MRs between Singapore to Australia (TC7) have dropped to just over $40,000/day from highs of $74,000/day. Gulf freight rates, where war risk sets the price, have held up comparatively well. Preliminary numbers show seaborne clean exports reaching 18.4 mbd in October, about 5% below the 2025 average. Gulf refinery runs appear to be picking up, which may explain part of the recent fall in crude exports. However, this is not yet visible in product loadings, and so far November data show little improvement, though subject to revisions”, Gibson said. Source: Gibson Shipbrokers Ltd The shipbroker added that “we see around 12% of the Aframax/LR2 fleet trading clean, near record lows. MRs have filled the gap, which lifted 55% of all clean cargo in October against 48% in 2025. Arguably little has supported clean tanker earnings more this year than dirty ups, and with dirty earnings still well above clean in most regions, that support does not yet seem at risk. Meanwhile, so far 116 MRs and 73 LR2s have delivered this year, more than in all of 2025, with a further 163 MRs (8% of the fleet) and 82 LR2s (11% of the fleet) scheduled to deliver between now and the end of 2027. We estimate that the recent surge in vessel attacks, especially in and around the Strait of Hormuz, has seen around 15 clean tankers attacked in October and early November, taking some capacity out of the market, at least temporarily”. Meanwhile, Gibson noted that “another factor to watch is China. Chinese CPP exports fell by around a quarter in October from September’s 1.1 mbd to around 850kbd. There are close to 16 million tonnes of quota left for the final two months, and November export plans are up 25%. However, so far preliminary clean export volumes are down, with loadings in the first half of the month running below October, and with landed refining margins this narrow the plans may not be met in full. For clean tankers, weaker margins could threaten both sides of the balance; fewer cargoes if refiners trim runs, and more ships if LR2s return from dirty trades. Demand projections have been drifting lower, with the IEA now seeing gasoline and diesel demand in 2027 around 1 mbd below 2025 levels. Deferred US maintenance is likely to fall in the first half of 2027, when El Niño could bring renewed Panama Canal restrictions and tighten MR supply in the Americas. For now, much rests on how many LR2s stay dirty, how much of its quota China uses, the potential of disruptive winter weather, and whether higher Gulf refinery runs start to show up in product exports”, the shipbroker concluded. articles.summary: Rates for shipping containers from east Asia and China to the US were mostly lower as the container shipping industry watches for a possible strike this weekend at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach (LA/LB), while liquid chem tanker rates ex-US Gulf were mostly higher. LA/LB STRIKE WATCH The possibility of a...
articles.body: Asia-US container rates lower, tanker rates ex-USG higher; possible strike at LA/LB ports this weekend in International Shipping News 23/11/2026 Rates for shipping containers from east Asia and China to the US were mostly lower as the container shipping industry watches for a possible strike this weekend at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach (LA/LB), while liquid chem tanker rates ex-US Gulf were mostly higher. LA/LB STRIKE WATCH The possibility of a strike this weekend at the ports of LA/LB grew after talks between International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 and the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) ended without an agreement. ILWU Local 26 is the union representing about 250 port watchmen at the ports of LA/LB, and PMA represents employers. Watchmen make up only 2% of ILWU workers at the two ports but work at terminals handling roughly 85% of Long Beach’s cargo and 33% of Los Angeles’ cargo. Should the watchmen strike, operations at eight terminals in the port complex could be brought to a halt as PMA expects other ILWU members would honor picket lines, potentially halting vessel, yard and gate operations at affected facilities. “With a strike vote already taken, the union has indicated an unwillingness to extend the contract beyond its expiration at 12:01 on Saturday, 21 November, setting up the real potential for a strike at the nation’s busiest port complex,” the PMA said in a statement on Wednesday. Judah Levine, head of research at online shipping marketplace and platform provider Freightos, said the timing would likely not affect Black Friday goods, which at this point for most importers would have had to be off yard already to arrive in time. “But other holiday season inventory is likely still at the port waiting to move inland, with perhaps more than usual as a significant rail backlog is impacting some of the rail terminals,” Levine said. “A work slowdown or stoppage would make that situation worse and threaten some holiday deliveries for some shippers.” Robert Khachatryan, founder and CEO of global logistics company Freight Right, said they are tracking the potential strike but have not been overly concerned. “This is a small group of employees and while the negotiations set the expectation for the next big one, we don’t think it is likely to cause major disruption,” Khachatryan said. CONTAINER RATES Rates to the West Coast are between $7,025-8,460/FEU (40-foot equivalent unit) while rates to the East Coast are between $8,194-10,900/FEU, trending lower from the highest rates seen since mid-2022 for both routes. Rates from Freightos showed slight increases this week, driven by delays in moving containers inland by rail. Levine said 1 November general rate increases (GRIs) did not stick, and that mid-month price increase initiatives also may not take. Carriers are continuing to manage capacity with blanked sailings and are also likely to announce 1 December GRIs. Levine said these price bumps could be more likely to materialize if supported by pre-Lunar New Year demand. Rates from supply chain advisors Drewry fell by 5% from Shanghai to Los Angeles, to the lowest in 12 weeks, and by 9% from Shanghai to New York, to the lowest in 15 weeks, as shown in the following graph. Drewry said carriers have announced 10 blanked sailings for the coming week after there were only four during the previous week. Despite these capacity reductions, Drewry expects freight rates to decrease further next week. Rates from ocean and freight rates and analytics firm Xeneta fell by almost 2% to the West Coast and by 3.1% to the East Coast. Peter Sand, Xeneta chief analyst, said offered capacity is increasing on all front hauls out of Asia-Pacific to Europe and the US. Rates on the Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI), which tracks rates for containers leaving Shanghai, fell by 1.92%, falling for the third week in a row. Rates on the NYSHEX Freight Index (NYFI) fell by 4.1% to the West Coast and by 8.3% to the East Coast. Container ships and costs for shipping containers are relevant to the chemical industry because while most chemicals are liquids and are shipped in tankers, container ships transport polymers, such as polyethylene (PE) and polypropylene (PP), which are shipped in pellets. Titanium dioxide (TiO2) is also shipped in containers. They also transport liquid chemicals in isotanks. LIQUID TANKER RATES Overall, US chemical tanker freight rates were largely mixed this week with the exceptions being the USG-to-ARA and USG-to-Brazil trade lanes, as those markets picked up this week following recent tightening. For the USG to ARA, several mid-size parcels of styrene were quoted or fixed in the market. Additionally, the larger size parcels mainly saw methanol and ethanol more frequently discussed. On the other hand, most owners are fairly booked for the rest of the month, leaving charterers already planning for December, while searching for caustic soda and styrene options. Part space has limited availability as most owners are awaiting COA (contract of affreightment) nominations although they already see high COA volumes, leaving little to no space available for spot transactions. Additionally, along the USG-to-Brazil route it was a decent week as several inquiries emerged, but as of now no fixtures were reported. Owners have reported limited space for parcel sized cargoes to both coasts of South America. However, rates remain pressured higher amid low volumes of fixtures rather than an uptick in demand. Ethanol, caustic soda, lube oil and MEG/DEG were all quoted for December dates. On the USG-to-Asia route, COA volumes continue to dominate any available tonnage, therefore rates remain steady, with little sign of easing in the near term. However, there could be upward pressure as most owners are looking to fill any available space. COA volumes remain firm, leaving very little available space, and most of the interest seems to be focused on southeast Asia. Activity in the market was driven primarily by larger methanol, ethanol, and glycol cargo movements, which made up most of the vessel-fixing activity. Meanwhile, demand for smaller chemical parcel shipments remained subdued, indicating weaker interest in smaller-volume cargoes. Along the USG-to-India trade lane, the route experienced another solid week of spot interest, although COA nominations continue to support any activity. Most regular carriers have filled up any available space rather quickly, which has attracted outsiders to enter this lane, keeping rates steady for the time being. There continues to be interest in various glycols and ethanol cargoes. Bunker prices were mixed, mainly due to the volatility in energy prices following cautious market sentiments. PANAMA CANAL CONDITIONS Weather conditions continue to improve in Central America, and the Panama Canal Authority (PCA) is immediately expanding daily capacity and raising the maximum authorized draft to 50 feet at the vital waterway. The following table shows daily capacity for booking dates that began on 12 November. One of the reasons the PCA acted is because of weather projections and improved water levels in Gatun Lake. Current water levels in the lake, which provides the freshwater necessary to operate the canal’s locks that lift and lower ships between sea level and lake level, are slightly above the 10-year average. articles.summary: Capesize The market endured a mixed and generally softer week, with early weakness in the Pacific weighing on sentiment before a midweek recovery helped steady the overall picture. The BCI 182 5TC fluctuated throughout the week, recovering some of its early losses midweek before easing again towards Friday,...
articles.body: Dry Bulk Market: Capesizes Trending Lower in Dry Bulk Market , International Shipping News 23/11/2026 C apesize The market endured a mixed and generally softer week, with early weakness in the Pacific weighing on sentiment before a midweek recovery helped steady the overall picture. The BCI 182 5TC fluctuated throughout the week, recovering some of its early losses midweek before easing again towards Friday, ultimately finishing $507 below Monday’s opening level. In the Pacific, C5 eased from $13.81 at the start of the week to a low of $13.40, before recovering to the $14.20–14.30 range by Thursday and ending the week at $14.40. The recovery was supported by strong miner participation, particularly on Wednesday, when all the major miners were active. The Atlantic remained more challenging, although the South Atlantic showed some resilience midweek as a tightening ballast list supported improved fixing activity around $35.00–35.25 on C3. This proved difficult to sustain, however, with rates subsequently coming under pressure and a wide spread between bids and offers highlighting continued uncertainty. Most first-half December cargoes have now been covered, with attention gradually shifting towards the second-half window. The North Atlantic remained the weakest area, with limited fresh demand, softer transatlantic fixtures and a lengthening tonnage list continuing to weigh on sentiment. Overall, the Pacific provided some welcome support and sentiment improved from the early-week lows, but persistent weakness across the North Atlantic and a lack of sustained momentum in the South Atlantic continued to limit the broader market’s recovery. Panamax-Kamsarmax Atlantic strength continued to offset softer Pacific conditions this week. North Atlantic activity picked up, with limited prompt tonnage and healthy mineral enquiry supporting owners’ expectations, while transatlantic grain rates edged higher. From the US East Coast, an 82,000-dwt fixed a transatlantic trip at $17,250 and an 81,000-dwt fixed to India at $28,000. EC South America remained well supported, with tight tonnage for first-half December arrivals helping to firm sentiment for later laycans. A 76,000-dwt, 77,000-dwt and 82,000-dwt fixed fronthaul trips at $17,200, $21,000 and $20,000 respectively, all basis delivery WC India. Conversely, slowing Australian mineral demand, limited North Pacific grain enquiry and growing tonnage availability continued to pressure Pacific rates. An 82,000-dwt fixed a North Pacific grain round at $19,250, with another 82,000-dwt fixing Australia to Taiwan at $20,900. Indonesian business also softened amid competition from older tonnage, with a 76,000-dwt fixing at $13,750. Period activity remained evident, with an 82,000-dwt fixing for one year at $21,500, scrubber benefit to charterers, while an 81,000-dwt secured $19,260 for a similar duration. Ultramax/Supramax It seemed like a week of consolidation, or possibly a turning point, with the market only slightly down overall from last week. The declining rates in the Pacific appeared to slow with some improved trades reported in the North during the second half of the week, with two 64,000-dwt modern types fixed from North China to West Africa at $25,100 and $25,250 respectively, and a newbuilding ex yard said to have agreed $24,500 for a NoPac round voyage. There were also two 60,000-dwt vessels fixed from North China to the US Gulf at around $19,000 and a 63,000-dwt from South China agreed $30,750 for a trip to Bangladesh. These were all positive indications, while, by comparison, Southeast Asia continued to struggle, with rates under pressure from ballasters arriving from the Indian Ocean. There wasn’t much movement in the Atlantic, with the Continent remaining firm, driven by scrap demand with a 63,000-dwt fixed from Bremen to the East Mediterranean at $32,000. The Mediterranean had a quiet week with few reported trades, but the South Atlantic was active with rates nudging up due to limited tonnage availability on early dates. articles.title: IEA: Extreme Weather Risks to International Oil and Natural Gas Shipping
articles.summary: International shipping is indispensable to oil and natural gas trade: in 2024, around 40% of crude oil, 30% of petroleum products, and 15% of natural gas supply made part of its journey to consumers by water. Yet this transport mode is exposed to risks from natural hazards, and specifically extreme weather events,...
articles.body: IEA: Extreme Weather Risks to International Oil and Natural Gas Shipping in International Shipping News 23/11/2026 I nternational shipping is indispensable to oil and natural gas trade: in 2024, around 40% of crude oil, 30% of petroleum products, and 15% of natural gas supply made part of its journey to consumers by water. Yet this transport mode is exposed to risks from natural hazards, and specifically extreme weather events, that can disrupt flows and undermine energy security. This report assesses how extreme weather risks affect international oil and natural gas shipping and how they could evolve in coming decades. Extreme weather can damage port infrastructure, interrupt operations, and restrict or close routes, forcing costly delays or diversions. Unlike other parts of the energy system, such as power outages where interruptions have an immediate impact, international fuel shipping is a relatively slow means of energy delivery. Interruptions take time to affect supply and markets, while consumers can draw on stocks if available should fuel deliveries be delayed. Nevertheless, depending on the location, severity and length of disruption, impacts have the potential to be severe and far-reaching. Maritime crude oil trade volumes have risen by around 15% since 2000 as refinery capacity and crude oil import demand shifts from the Atlantic Basin towards Asia. liquefied natural gas (LNG) volumes have quadrupled over the same period as new export capacity in Australia, the United States and elsewhere feeds growing Asian demand. Reliance on shipping is set to increase. In the IEA’s Stated Policies Scenario, international oil and natural gas shipping activity rises by over 15% by 2035, with LNG growing faster than oil. Growth is stronger in the Current Policies Scenario, underpinned by slower progress in efficiency and clean energy deployment. In either scenario, the resilience of ports, their terminals and shipping routes become more important as greater fuel volumes are channelled through shipping’s network of physical nodes and trading corridors. Port infrastructure is exposed to extreme weather hazards including flooding, high winds and extreme heat, depending on location. Virtually all ports with regular tanker activity in Japan, Korea and China are exposed to a tropical cyclone at least once in 500 years on average. The US Gulf Coast, where nearly half of the country’s refining capacity is located, is also exposed to tropical cyclones and the flooding they can cause. Tanker-handling ports experience an average downtime of 1.5 days per year due to disruption from extreme weather, with around 60% of assessed ports losing less than one day annually. Yet individual high-impact events can cause substantially longer disruptions, with ports shut for weeks or even months, before operations are. Physical damage is also material. Research estimates current annual weather-related physical damage to tanker-handling ports at around USD 5 billion, with Europe and North America accounting for nearly half of this due to the number and value of assets exposed. By 2050, annual damage could nearly double in the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) scenario associated with around 3 °C warming by the end of the century. River flooding accounts for around half of current estimated damage, while coastal flooding becomes a larger driver in the future as sea-level rise compounds with the risk of storm surge that tropical cyclones can cause. Maritime trade routes are more vulnerable when they are concentrated through chokepoints that limit alternative options. Extreme weather disruption risk depends on location. For example, tropical cyclones can disrupt the Luzon Strait between the South China and Philippine seas; fog can temporarily close the Turkish Straits connecting the Mediterranean and Black seas; and drought can constrain Panama Canal transits for months. Where rerouting is possible, disruption raises voyage times, fuel use, freight costs and emissions; where practical alternatives are limited, disruption can stop flows altogether. Some inland shipping routes face disruption from drought, which lowers water levels and limits navigability. Ships may need to reduce their draught by shedding load, reducing capacity and increasing costs. In more severe cases shippers may need to find alternative routes overland by road or rail. At Kaub on the River Rhine, between 2015 and 2026 navigation was economically unviable for around one month per year on average. In the IPCC scenario associated with global warming of above 3 °C, this could double to nearly two months by the end of the century. Geography shapes the distribution of shipping infrastructure and routes, sometimes resulting in concentrations of ports that can be vulnerable to single weather events. Port clusters can provide regional flexibility to manage disruption, but also vulnerability should a region-wide event knock multiple ports offline. The influence of geography applies at a small scale too. Many small island economies depend heavily on imported fuels via one or two import terminals, and face acute disruption if flows are interrupted. IEA analysis of selected fuel-importing small island economies finds that over 85% rely on imported fossil fuels for at least three-quarters of power generation. Yet fuel stocks may be limited: more than 15% of small islands in the dataset hold less than 90 days of fuel supply, while six hold as little as three weeks. Strengthening the resilience of international fuel shipping requires action across governance, monitoring, operations, port construction and system design. Measures include disaster management frameworks, flood defences and the stockpiling of critical spares. Cooperation across stakeholders can further bolster the resilience of international oil and natural gas shipping. Key actions • Incorporate extreme weather resilience into energy security planning. Countries should consider the impacts of disruption on their shipped energy trade flows as part of national energy strategies and emergency plans, and with consideration for projected changes in operating conditions. • Diversify energy sources and supply chains. Broadening the mix of energy sources reduces the risk of serious impact should flow from any single source be disrupted. This action brings wider energy security benefits beyond addressing risk from extreme weather, as disruption risk from other causes such as conflict, malicious attacks or geopolitics can also be mitigated. • Enhance operations across energy shipping infrastructure. Through operational systems and processes, strengthen the ability to maintain energy flows when infrastructure assets or supply routes are disrupted. • Take measures to increase infrastructure robustness. Prioritise cost-effective measures by considering actions that could be taken to mitigate risk such as flood protection, resilient electricity and communications systems, elevated critical equipment, and protection against wind and waves. • Strengthen early warning and operational preparedness. Leverage meteorological and oceanographic data and modelling for better anticipation of extreme weather conditions. • Address the acute vulnerability of small island economies. Support adequate fuel reserves, resilient import infrastructure, emergency recovery plans and regional assistance arrangements; develop domestic energy sources such as renewables to reduce dependence on imported fuels. • Deepen international cooperation and information sharing. Share data for better risk assessment across industry and countries; develop regionally coordinated management and responses to disruptions such as stockpiling of spare parts. • Foster international recognition and cooperation to limit trade route disruption. Build consensus to support better management of trade routes, especially chokepoints and inland waterways where disruption can have far-reaching consequences. Source: IEA Tops 2026-11-23 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.body: VLCC Market Moved Higher Last Week in International Shipping News 23/11/2026 Clean LR2 LR2 performance was mixed this week, with a sharp rise in eastbound Middle East Gulf rates contrasting with softer westbound and Mediterranean routes. TC1 (75kt MEG/Japan) climbed 36 points to WS1049, lifting the Baltic round-trip TCE by $11,400 to $308,200/day. Conversely, TC20 (90kt MEG/UK-Continent) eased by $378,600 to $18.64 million, corresponding to a Baltic round-trip TCE of $287,600/day. TC15 (80kt Mediterranean/East) also softened, declining $100,000 to $7.66 million, with the TCE slipping $1,300 to $60,100/day. LR1 LR1 rates were comparatively stable, particularly on the eastbound Middle East Gulf trade. TC5 (55kt MEG/Japan) remained broadly unchanged at WS993, equating to a Baltic round-trip TCE of $206,800/day. Westbound, TC8 (65kt MEG/UK-Continent) edged $78,600 lower to $14.56 million, with the corresponding TCE easing $1,000 to $222,200/day. MR MR markets weakened across the board, with the most pronounced losses centred on the US Gulf and the wider Atlantic market. TC17 (35kt MEG/East Africa) declined around 12 points to WS913, reducing the TCE by $1,900 to $117,600/day. On the UK Continent, TC2 (37kt ARA/US Atlantic Coast) fell 19 points to WS184, with the Baltic round-trip TCE declining $3,400 to $11,300/day. Pressure was considerably stronger in the US Gulf. TC14 (38kt US Gulf/UK-Continent) fell sharply by 121 points to WS237, cutting the round-trip TCE by $24,100 to $23,700/day. TC21 (38kt US Gulf/Caribbean) recorded a similarly substantial decline, falling $470,800 to $762,500 and reducing the Baltic TCE by $27,300 to $20,100/day. The broader deterioration in Atlantic earnings was reflected in the MR Atlantic Triangulation Basket TCE, which fell from $60,600/day to $37,000/day. Handymax Handymax performance diverged between the Mediterranean and UK Continent markets. In the Mediterranean, TC6 (30kt Cross-Mediterranean) strengthened by 30 points to WS399, lifting the Baltic round-trip TCE by $9,300 to $76,100/day. In contrast, TC23 (30kt Cross UK-Continent) declined 23 points to WS394, with the corresponding TCE falling $6,500 to $72,700/day. VLCC VLCC rates on the Baltic Exchange strengthened across most routes this week. TD3C (270,000 mt Middle East Gulf/China) rose 21.25 points to WS315.63, generating a daily round-trip TCE of $1,079,794 for the standard Baltic VLCC. TD34 (Gulf of Oman/China) was comparatively stable, edging just over a point higher to WS309.38, equating to a round-trip TCE of $305,337/day. In the Atlantic, sentiment was more mixed. The 260,000 mt West Africa/China route (TD15) eased 4.29 points to WS293.57, corresponding to a round-trip TCE of $272,771/day. Conversely, the US Gulf/China route (TD22) advanced by $2.5 million to approximately $34.5 million, lifting the daily round-trip TCE to $253,509/day. Suezmax The Suezmax market firmed broadly across the Baltic Exchange routes this week. The 130,000 mt Nigeria/UK Continent route (TD20) advanced 22.56 points to WS330.56, equating to a daily round-trip TCE of approximately $165,677. TD27 (130,000 mt Guyana/UK Continent) strengthened by 14.73 points to WS332.06, returning just under $163,800/day. The most pronounced increase was recorded on the 145,000 mt US Gulf/UK Continent route (TD33), which gained more than 37 points to WS306.67, with the corresponding TCE rising to just over $184,800/day. In the Black Sea, the 135,000 mt CPC/Augusta route (TD6) softened to WS416.33 midweek before recovering to WS426.11 at the time of writing, equating to a daily round-trip TCE of just over $306,900. Aframax The Aframax market strengthened sharply this week, with exceptional gains across the Atlantic routes accompanied by firming in the North Sea and Mediterranean, while Vancouver exports were comparatively subdued. In the North Sea, the 80,000 mt Cross-UK Continent route (TD7) advanced 40.83 points to WS288.33, equating to a daily round-trip TCE of just under $183,937, basis Hound Point/Wilhelmshaven. In the Mediterranean, TD19 (80,000 mt Cross-Mediterranean) posted a stronger gain of 84.44 points to WS352.22, returning approximately $134,100/day on a Ceyhan/Lavera basis. The most pronounced moves were seen across the Atlantic, where Aframax rates surged significantly higher. TD26 (70,000 mt East Coast Mexico/US Gulf) climbed almost 310 points to WS631.11, generating a daily round-trip TCE of just over $219,200. TD9 (70,000 mt Covenas/US Gulf) recorded a similarly sharp increase, gaining 311 points to around WS623 and returning just over $197,400/day. TD25 (70,000 mt US Gulf/UK Continent) was also assessed 283 points higher at just over WS596, equating to approximately $180,100/day on a Houston/Rotterdam basis. By comparison, the Vancouver export routes were considerably more stable. TD28 (80,000 mt Vancouver/China) eased by $200,000 to $8.17 million, corresponding to a round-trip TCE of approximately $162,000/day. TD29 (80,000 mt Vancouver/Pacific Area Lightering point off the US West Coast) slipped four points to WS683. Source: Baltic Exchange 2026-11-23 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share

articles.title: Two Supply Lines, One Terminal: 12 Sanctioned Tankers at the Houthi-Controlled Ras Issa
articles.summary: Between September 16 and November 7, 2026, Windward MIOC identified 12 sanctioned tankers delivering fuel to Ras Issa, the Houthi-controlled oil terminal on Yemen’s Red Sea coast, together carrying an estimated 3.26 million barrels. Eleven of the twelve had their AIS switched off when Windward found them. Five...
articles.body: Two Supply Lines, One Terminal: 12 Sanctioned Tankers at the Houthi-Controlled Ras Issa in International Shipping News 23/11/2026 Between September 16 and November 7, 2026, Windward MIOC identified 12 sanctioned tankers delivering fuel to Ras Issa, the Houthi-controlled oil terminal on Yemen’s Red Sea coast, together carrying an estimated 3.26 million barrels. Eleven of the twelve had their AIS switched off when Windward found them. Five broadcast false positions ranging from 80 to 2,800 nautical miles away. All 12 were already sanctioned. Eleven of them carry U.S. designations. Tracing the cargo back from the terminal, Windward found two distinct supply lines, one carrying Russian diesel and other fuels south through the Suez Canal, and one carrying Iranian-origin cargo out of the Middle East Gulf. This brief sets out what Windward identified across each supply line and how the tankers concealed themselves. The two supply lines Windward identified into Ras Issa run north from Russia via Suez and south from Iran via Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb. Tracks are schematic. Source: Windward Maritime AI™ Platform. What Happened Twelve Sanctioned Tankers, Eleven of Them Dark Across the seven-week window, Windward identified 12 sanctioned tankers at the Houthi-controlled Ras Issa terminal and the nearby Salif anchorage. All 12 were already on sanctions lists at the time of identification, 11 of them under U.S. programs. Five were designated under counter-terrorism (SDGT), four under the Iran program, four under Russia programs across U.S., UK, and EU lists, and one under the Venezuela program. Two tankers carry both Iran and Russia sanctions. Three were sanctioned specifically for supplying Ras Issa, and eight were repeat suppliers to Ras Issa or Yemen. The average vessel age was 25 years, with two built in 1993. The 12 tankers sailed under 11 different flags, including the landlocked states of Malawi, Mali, and Botswana. Eleven of the twelve had their AIS switched off while at the terminal. Five broadcast false positions while sitting off Ras Issa, ranging from 80 nautical miles away (mid-Red Sea) to 2,800 nautical miles away (between Sri Lanka and Malaysia). Cargo on two of the tankers reached Ras Issa through chains of ship-to-ship transfers. One tanker has been dark since May 30, 2026. At least four additional tankers were seen at the anchorage on November 7 and have not yet been identified. The Northern Supply Line: Russian Diesel Through Three Transfers The northern supply line carried fuel south from Russia’s Black Sea ports through the Suez Canal, with cargo frequently changing hands off Port Said or in the Gulf of Suez before moving down the Red Sea to Ras Issa. Six of the 12 tankers took this route, carrying an estimated 1.57 million barrels between them. The route carries more than Russian cargo. Gulf-loaded gasoline also changes hands at the northern transfer points before heading south. One case illustrates the pattern end to end: On June 9, about 130,400 barrels of Russian diesel was loaded at Taman onto a Russian-flagged tanker sanctioned under Russia programs. Between September 11 and 20, the cargo passed through three ship-to-ship transfers, one off Port Said and two in the Gulf of Suez, each between Russian-flagged tankers sanctioned under Russia programs. Cargo data and draught changes matched at every step. The final tanker in the chain, ASTRA (IMO 9296585), a U.S.- and UK-sanctioned Russian-flagged product tanker built in 2005, carried the cargo south. It anchored off Djibouti for 17.5 days, declared “SUEZ” as its destination and turned north while still laden, then went dark 39 nautical miles from Ras Issa on October 14 and stayed dark for 26 days. Windward identified it at the Ras Issa mooring buoy on high-resolution imagery between October 30 and November 5, with a floating hose alongside, consistent with discharge. Electro-optical imagery matched it again in port on November 5. It reappeared on AIS on November 9, 180 nautical miles north of Ras Issa, heading up the Red Sea. Satellite imagery matching ASTRA to the Ras Issa berth on November 5, 2026, against its reference image from September 26. Source: Windward Remote Sensing Intelligence. One tanker on the northern route is the sole fully AIS-visible vessel among the 12. MD MIRANDA (IMO 9198290), a Gambia-flagged product tanker built in 1999, is sanctioned by the UK and EU as part of Russia’s shadow fleet under Russia programs. It made three Ras Issa port calls in 2026, in February, March, and July. In April, it went dark for four days off Novorossiysk, then sailed back via the Bosporus and Suez to Ras Issa, most likely with Russian cargo. MD MIRANDA broadcast openly from the Salif anchorage throughout the observation window. The Southern Supply Line: Iranian LPG Through the Strait of Hormuz The southern supply line carried Iranian LPG out of the Middle East Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz, across the Arabian Sea, and into the Red Sea through Bab el-Mandeb. Five of the 12 tankers took this route, carrying an estimated 1.3 million barrels. Three of those tankers were LPG carriers that loaded in Iran and were later identified in the Ras Issa area. Together they carried about 770,000 barrels of LPG. All three were sanctioned, and all three were dark when Windward identified them at the terminal. The clearest case is SARAH (IMO 9014420), a Comoros-flagged LPG carrier built in 1993. SARAH was designated by OFAC under the counter-terrorism SDGT program in April 2025 for supplying LPG to Ras Issa. Windward assesses that SARAH discharged at Ras Issa on November 5. On August 2, 2026, it entered the Middle East Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz. Its AIS sent 46 positions at 0°N 0°E, indicating GPS jamming, over 3.3 hours before reappearing in Iranian territorial waters 44 nautical miles further on. It then anchored for about 10 days off Bandar Imam Khomeini while broadcasting an Iraqi destination. On August 15, it loaded about 114,600 barrels of LPG in Iran, declaring Kamaran, the island off Ras Issa, as its first destination before changing to Iraq. On August 16 and 17, Windward observed impossible position jumps off the United Arab Emirates as it exited the Strait of Hormuz. Its AIS never went off. It broadcast false positions throughout. On November 5, Windward identified SARAH dark at the Ras Issa terminal berth, while its AIS placed it anchored off Shinas, Oman, more than 1,500 nautical miles away by sea. Satellite imagery matching SARAH to the Ras Issa berth on November 5, 2026, against its reference image from September 11. Source: Windward Remote Sensing Intelligence. Two other LPG carriers loaded in Iran contributed the remaining volume. One loaded about 521,000 barrels on May 31 while declaring a destination in China. The other loaded about 133,800 barrels on August 19, declaring Kamaran, and crossed Bab el-Mandeb with its AIS off. Across all three tankers, about 770,000 barrels of Iranian LPG reached the Ras Issa area during the observation window. An Estimated 3.26 Million Barrels Across Seven Weeks Across the 12 identified tankers, Windward estimates total deliveries at about 3.26 million barrels. About 1.94 million barrels is confirmed by wet-cargo data for seven of the tankers. The remaining 1.31 million barrels is estimated for the other five, using deadweight at 95% capacity and seven barrels per ton, counted at half to reflect the part-laden pattern seen in the tankers with known cargo. One tanker in the set that had known cargo carried about 40% of capacity; another carried about a third. The estimate assumes each tanker discharged its full cargo at Ras Issa and counts each tanker once. Roughly half the fuel came down from the north, and four in ten came up from the south. One tanker’s origin is undetermined, carrying an estimated 391,000 barrels. By fuel type, Iranian LPG accounted for about 769,000 barrels, Middle East Gulf (potentially Iranian) gasoline for about 585,000, fuel oil for about 176,000, and Russian-origin diesel traced end to end for about 130,400. About 1.6 million barrels moved on tankers whose cargo type was not independently confirmed. A Houthi-controlled floating storage tanker anchored three nautical miles off the terminal has received at least one million barrels of mostly Russian-origin products, according to Lloyd’s List. A Congested Terminal Wait times between arrival and discharge ranged from two and a half weeks to more than five months. One tanker has been anchored off Ras Issa, dark, since the end of May 2026. Another was seen in the area 12 times over 60 days. A third waited about four weeks before it moored at the terminal. The queue points to limited discharge capacity at Ras Issa since the 2025 strikes, and the predictability it creates makes the anchorage a reliable place to find the vessels operating on this route. How Windward Identified Them An AIS-only view of the Ras Issa terminal across this seven-week window would have shown one tanker: MD MIRANDA, broadcasting openly from the Salif anchorage. Windward identified more. The gap between the one and the twelve is what this report is about, and it rests on four capabilities applied together. The first is identifying dark vessels from satellite imagery. Eleven of the twelve tankers had their AIS switched off at the terminal and were identified by matching dark hulls in high-resolution and satellite imagery against known vessel references, a capability powered by Windward Remote Sensing Intelligence. The matching rests on sophisticated algorithms developed by Windward MIOC that compare hull geometry, length-to-beam ratios, deck features, and shadow signatures against a reference library of known vessels. Candidates that do not meet strict confidence criteria are omitted. ASTRA was identified at the Ras Issa mooring buoy for over 26 days with its AIS off. SARAH was identified at the Ras Issa berth on November 5 while its AIS placed it more than 1,500 nautical miles away. The remaining three capabilities cross-check and enrich what the imagery surfaces. The second is tracking cargo from where it is loaded to where it is delivered, including across ship-to-ship transfer chains. Windward followed about 130,400 barrels of Russian diesel from the Taman loading on June 9, through three Russian-flagged tankers sanctioned under Russia programs, to ASTRA. Cargo data and draught changes matched at every step. The same approach followed three LPG cargoes totaling about 770,000 barrels from loading in Iran to the Ras Issa area. The third is detecting falsified AIS. A vessel broadcasting openly can still be reporting a false position, and five of the 12 did so. SARAH broadcast as anchored off Shinas, Oman, while imagery placed it at the Ras Issa berth more than 1,500 nautical miles away. Impossible position jumps, fixed positions in open ocean, and declared destinations inconsistent with cargo records are the signatures Windward tracked across the five. The fourth is the fusion of these inputs with analyst review. Satellite imagery, coastal camera intelligence, wet-cargo data, and AIS behavior analytics each show a part of the picture. The 12 identifications hold because each was built from more than one source and reviewed by MIOC analysts. What It Signals Across the two supply lines, the ownership picture is where the Russian and Iranian lines diverge most sharply. Four of the 12 tankers at Ras Issa, plus three in the transfer chain that delivered cargo to ASTRA, are sanctioned under Russia programs. The Houthi-controlled floating storage anchored off the terminal has received mostly Russian-origin products, per Lloyd’s List. Windward assesses that this pattern may reflect Russian state-tolerated or coordinated support for the Houthis. One possible motive is safe passage through Bab el-Mandeb for Russian-linked shipping, consistent with publicly reported Houthi assurances to Russian-linked vessels. Confidence is low to moderate, as Windward sees vessels, cargo, and routes, not intent. The Iranian supply line runs on a different playbook. The cargo is predominantly Iranian LPG. The tankers are already sanctioned for moving Iranian- or Houthi-bound fuel. The concealment pattern is consistent across the three tankers. They used falsified AIS rather than switched-off AIS through the Strait of Hormuz, declared false destinations in Iraq and China, and went dark across Bab el-Mandeb. Windward assesses that the Iranian line is resilient and adaptive, and its vessel movements cannot be followed on AIS alone. Source: Windward 2026-11-23 hellenicshippingnews... tweet Share
takeaways: Eleven of the twelve had their AIS switched off when Windward found them.
Five broadcast false positions ranging from 80 to 2,800 nautical miles away.
This brief sets out what Windward identified across each supply line and how the tankers concealed themselves.
