articles.body: Dynagas LNG Reports Higher Earnings, Tempered By Yamal Sanctions And Insurance Risk in Hellenic Shipping News 23/11/2026 Dynagas LNG Partners LP, an owner of liquefied natural gas (“LNG”) carriers, announced its results for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026. Nine Months Highlights: Net Income and Earnings per common unit (basic and diluted) of $51.9 million and $1.29, respectively; Adjusted Net Income(1) of $46.6 million and Adjusted Earnings per common unit(1) (basic and diluted) of $1.14; Adjusted EBITDA(1) of $82.0 million; and 97.1% fleet utilization(2). Quarter Highlights: Net Income and Earnings per common unit (basic and diluted) of $18.6 million and $0.46, respectively; Adjusted Net Income(1) of $18.4 million and Adjusted Earnings per common unit(1) (basic and diluted) of $0.46; Adjusted EBITDA(1) of $30.1 million; 100% fleet utilization(2); The Arctic Aurora was delivered under its new time charter party agreement with Rio Grande LNG, LLC (“Rio Grande”) on September 15, 2026; Declared and paid a cash distribution of $0.5625 per unit on the Partnership’s Series A Preferred Units (NYSE: DLNG PR A) for the period from May 12, 2026 to August 11, 2026; and Declared a quarterly cash distribution of $0.050 per common unit for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, which was paid on August 28, 2026, to all common unitholders of record as of August 24, 2026. Recent Events: On November 12, 2026, the Partnership completed the partial redemption of its Series A Preferred Units, redeeming 2,000,000 of its 3,000,000 outstanding Series A Preferred Units, which was announced on October 9, 2026, at a redemption price of $25.00 per unit, or $50.0 million in aggregate. Following the partial redemption, 1,000,000 Series A Preferred Units remain outstanding; Declared a quarterly cash distribution of $0.5625 per unit on the Partnership’s Series A Preferred Units for the period from August 12, 2026 to November 11, 2026, which was paid on November 12, 2026 to all Series A Preferred unitholders of record as of November 4, 2026; and Declared a quarterly cash distribution of $0.050 per common unit for the quarter ended September 30, 2026, which is payable on November 20, 2026 to all common unitholders of record as of November 13, 2026. CEO Commentary: We are pleased to report a strong third quarter. Adjusted EBITDA rose 9.2% year on year to $30.1 million and Adjusted Net Income increased 29.3% to $18.4 million, as the fleet operated at 100% utilization and our fleet-wide Time Charter Equivalent (TCE) rate reached $75,027 per day, up 11.8% on the third quarter of 2025 and 7.0% on the previous quarter. This TCE comfortably exceeded our cash breakeven for the quarter of approximately $47,100 per day. The quarter benefited from the first full three months of the Clean Energy’s charter with Rio Grande and from a further 30.8% year-on-year reduction in net interest and finance costs. Commercially, the Arctic Aurora commenced its new time charter with Rio Grande on September 15, 2026, securing its employment until at least August 2033. With two of our six vessels now chartered to Rio Grande, alongside our long-standing charters with SEFE and Yamal Trade, our fleet is fully contracted for the remainder of 2026 and for 2027, and 65% contracted for 2028. As of the date of this release, our estimated contracted revenue backlog stands at $700 million, with an average remaining contract term of 4.2 years. Our balance sheet continued to strengthen. During the first nine months of 2026 we repaid $33.1 million of debt, reducing our outstanding financial liabilities to $245.6 million, while our cash increased to $79.9 million at September 30, 2026 from $41.0 million at the end of 2025. At the same time, we continued to return capital to our unitholders, maintaining our quarterly distribution of $0.050 per common unit and paying the full distributions on our Series A Preferred Units. After the quarter end, on November 12, 2026, we redeemed 2,000,000 of our Series A Preferred Units, two-thirds of the class, for $50.0 million, which reduces our annual preferred distributions by $4.5 million. Three Months Ended September 30, 2026 and 2025 Financial Results Net Income for the three months ended September 30, 2026 was $18.6 million as compared to $18.7 million for the corresponding period in 2025, which represents a decrease of $0.1 million, or 0.6%. The decrease in Net Income was mainly attributable to the Other income which was recognized in the third quarter of 2025, and the increase in Voyage expenses and Vessel operating expenses. The above decrease was substantially offset by (a) the increase in Voyage revenues and (b) the decrease in Net interest and finance costs as explained below. Adjusted Net Income (a non-GAAP financial measure) for the three months ended September 30, 2026 was $18.4 million, compared to $14.2 million for the corresponding period in 2025, which represents a net increase of $4.2 million, or 29.3%. This increase was mainly attributable to (a) the increase in cash Voyage revenues as explained below, and (b) the decrease in Net interest and finance costs which was partially offset by the increase in Vessel operating expenses. Voyage revenues for the three months ended September 30, 2026 were $44.0 million, compared to $38.9 million for the corresponding period in 2025, which represents a net increase of $5.1 million, or 13.1%. This increase was mainly attributable to: (a) the higher time charter rate earned by the Clean Energy under its time charter with Rio Grande, which commenced on April 30, 2026, (b) the increase in variable hire revenues earned under the OPEX pass-through time charters of the Yenisei River and the Lena River, (c) the increase in Revenue earning days, as the fleet operated at full utilization during the quarter compared to the corresponding period of 2025, (d) the non-cash effect of the amortization of deferred revenue, (e) a ballast bonus of $0.9 million due to the Partnership upon the redelivery of the Arctic Aurora by Equinor and (f) the increase of the value of the EU ETS emissions allowances (“EUAs”) due to the Partnership by the charterers of its vessels (the corresponding value of the EUAs, which the Partnership is obliged to surrender to the EU authorities, is included within Voyage expenses, therefore the net effect of the EUAs to the Operating Income and Net income is zero). The above increase was partially offset by the lower time charter rates earned by the Arctic Aurora under its charter with Equinor until September 15, 2026 and under its new time charter thereafter, compared to the corresponding period in 2025. The Partnership reported average daily hire gross of commissions(3) of approximately $74,820 per day per vessel for the three-month period ended September 30, 2026, compared to approximately $69,960 per day per vessel for the corresponding period in 2025. The Partnership’s vessels operated at 100% and 99.1% fleet utilization during the three-month periods ended September 30, 2026 and 2025, respectively. Vessel operating expenses were $8.9 million, which corresponds to a daily rate per vessel of $16,121 for the three-month period ended September 30, 2026, compared to $8.1 million, or a daily rate per vessel of $14,594 in the corresponding period in 2025. This increase was mainly attributable to increased crew costs and higher repairs and maintenance costs. As mentioned above, a substantial part of the increase in Vessel operating expenses is counter-balanced by the corresponding increase in variable hire revenues earned on the Partnership’s vessels operating under OPEX pass-through time charters. Adjusted EBITDA (a non-GAAP financial measure) for the three months ended September 30, 2026 was $30.1 million, compared to $27.6 million for the corresponding period in 2025. The increase of $2.5 million, or 9.2%, was mainly attributable to the above-mentioned increase in cash Voyage revenues, which was partially offset by the increase in Vessel operating expenses. Net interest and finance costs were $3.7 million in the three months ended September 30, 2026, compared to $5.3 million in the corresponding period in 2025, which represents a decrease of $1.6 million, or 30.8%, mainly due to (i) the decrease in the interest on our Sale and Leaseback Agreements, as a result of the reduction in interest-bearing debt and the decrease in the weighted average interest rate from 6.50% in the three months ended September 30, 2025 to 5.94% in the three months ended September 30, 2026, (ii) the interest expense of $0.4 million on the Series B Preferred Units for the period from July 1, 2025 to their redemption date on July 25, 2025, which was included in the corresponding period of 2025, and (iii) the increase in interest income. For the three months ended September 30, 2026, the Partnership reported both basic and diluted Earnings per common unit and Adjusted Earnings per common unit (a non-GAAP financial measure), of $0.46, after taking into account the distributions relating to the Series A Preferred Units on the Partnership’s Net Income/Adjusted Net Income. Earnings per common unit and Adjusted Earnings per common unit, basic and diluted, were calculated on the basis of a weighted average number of 36,382,011 common units outstanding during the period and in the case of Adjusted Earnings per common unit, after reflecting the impact of certain adjustments presented in Appendix B of this press release. Adjusted Net Income, Adjusted EBITDA, and Adjusted Earnings per common unit are not recognized measures under U.S. GAAP. Please refer to Appendix B of this press release for the definitions and reconciliation of these measures to the most directly comparable financial measures calculated and presented in accordance with U.S. GAAP. Ltd. amounted to $34.3 million, $45.6 million, $46.8 million and $118.9 million, respectively, gross of unamortized deferred loan fees. The financial liabilities under the Sale and Leaseback Agreements are repayable in quarterly installments, with the final installments, including purchase obligation prices of $10.7 million, $14.2 million, $14.6 million and $22.1 million, respectively, due in June 2029 for the Clean Energy, the OB River and the Amur River and in June 2034 for the Arctic Aurora. Scheduled principal repayments for the twelve months ending September 30, 2027 amount to $44.2 million. On November 12, 2026, the Partnership paid $50.0 million for the partial redemption of its Series A Preferred Units described under “Recent Events” above. Vessel Employment As of November 20, 2026, the Partnership had estimated contracted time charter coverage(4) for 100%, 100% and 65% of its fleet estimated Available Days (as defined in Appendix B) for each of 2026, 2027 and 2028, respectively. As of the same date, the Partnership’s estimated contracted revenue backlog (5) (6) was $700 million, with an average remaining contract term of 4.2 years. Russian Sanctions Developments Due to the ongoing Russian war with Ukraine, the United Kingdom (the “U.K.”), the European Union (“E.U.”), the United States (“U.S.”) and other countries and organizations have publicly announced and enacted extensive sanctions against Russia to impose severe economic pressure on the Russian economy and government. Two of our vessels, the Yenisei River and Lena River (the “Vessels”), are employed by Yamal Trade Pte. Ltd. (the “Charterer”) under long-term time charters that extend to 2033 and 2034, respectively (the “Yamal Charters”). Since the commencement of the Yamal Charters, the Vessels have been engaged in the transportation of LNG produced in Russia for discharge at destinations worldwide (the “Yamal LNG Transportation”) in compliance with applicable sanctions regulations. U.K. Sanctions On May 20, 2026, the Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/543) came into force in the U.K., amending the Russia (Sanctions) (EU Exit) Regulations 2019. The amendments introduced new Regulations 46Z29B to 46Z29D, which prohibit U.K. persons from directly or indirectly supplying or delivering Russian-origin LNG by ship, and from providing or facilitating related services. The ban covers shipments from Russia to third countries as well as between third countries and is subject to limited exceptions and licensing arrangements. For supply contracts with a duration exceeding one year that were executed before June 17, 2025 and have not since been amended, other than by amendments falling within specified categories, there is a transitional exception that covers relevant activities carried out before January 1, 2027. As a result, following expiry of the applicable transitional exception, U.K.-based providers of financial services, including the insurers that currently provide protection and indemnity (“P&I”) and hull and machinery (“H&M”) insurance for the Vessels, will be prohibited from providing cover for voyages carrying Russian-origin LNG, unless an applicable exception or licence permits such cover. The U.K. prohibition does not extend to technical services, including classification. As of the date of this press release, discussions with alternative insurance providers are ongoing; however, we have not secured replacement P&I or H&M insurance for the Vessels and there can be no assurance that such insurance will be in place by January 1, 2027, or that it will be available on comparable terms, or at all. If such insurance is not in place, this could give rise to disputes under the Yamal Charters, including disputes concerning the respective rights and obligations of the Charterer and us under the Yamal Charters. Any such dispute could result in claims that the Vessels are off-hire, additional costs, loss of revenue, litigation or early termination of the Yamal Charters, among other things. Any of these developments could adversely affect our business, financial condition, results of operations, cash flows and our ability to make distributions to our unitholders and could result in an event of default under our debt agreements, among other things. E.U. Sanctions On October 23, 2025, the E.U. adopted the 19th package of sanctions (the “19th Package”), which prohibits the purchase, import or transfer, directly or indirectly, by E.U. persons and non-E.U. persons with an E.U.-nexus, of LNG that originates in Russia or is exported from Russia (the “LNG Prohibition”). The LNG Prohibition applies from January 1, 2027 with respect to supply contracts with a duration exceeding one year (“Long Term Contracts”) that were executed before June 17, 2025 and that have not since been amended, other than by amendments falling within specified categories. On July 23, 2026, the E.U. amended the 19th Package with the adoption of the 21st package of sanctions (the “21st Package”). The 21st Package introduced an exemption to the LNG Prohibition, initially until July 25, 2027, and thereafter for successive periods of one year, unless the Council of the E.U. (the “E.U. Council”), following an annual review, decides otherwise. The exemption applies to transfers of LNG destined for third countries and, where relevant, purchases associated with those transfers, pursuant to Long Term Contracts that were executed before February 24, 2022 and that have not since been amended, other than by amendments falling within specified categories, provided that the volume of LNG transferred each year under the exemption does not exceed the volume of LNG transferred in 2025 under its qualifying existing Long Term Contract, irrespective of destination (the “Legacy Contract Derogation”). We, and our sanctions counsel, believe that the transportation of LNG under the Yamal Charters to destinations outside the E.U. currently falls within the Legacy Contract Derogation and, accordingly, is outside the scope of the LNG Prohibition. However, there can be no absolute guaranteed assurance that our interpretation of the Legacy Contract Derogation is correct, or that regulatory authorities or our counterparties will agree with our interpretation. Furthermore, there can be no absolute guaranteed assurance that the transportation of LNG under the Yamal Charters will continue to meet the requirements of the Legacy Contract Derogation, including with respect to the yearly volume limitation, or that the E.U. Council will not decide, following an annual review, to shorten or terminate the Legacy Contract Derogation, or that sanctions regulations will not be further implemented, amended, or expanded to restrict the transportation of Russian-origin LNG. These risks are outside of our control, and if one or more of these events were to occur, the Vessels would be restricted from transporting LNG originating in or exported from Russia, which would affect the Charterer’s ability to continue employing the Vessels in the Yamal LNG Transportation. Notwithstanding the foregoing, we believe the Yamal Charters would remain enforceable, although their sanctions-specific provisions may suspend performance and, at a later stage, payment of charter hire. The Charterer may not agree with our interpretation, which could result in disputes, Charterer non-performance, litigation or early termination of the Yamal Charters, among other things. Any of these developments would have a material adverse effect on our business, results of operations, financial condition, cash flows and our ability to make distributions to our unitholders and could result in an event of default under our debt agreements, among other things. U.S. Sanctions On September 18, 2026, the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 (the “Graham Act”) was enacted in the U.S. Among other things, the Graham Act authorizes the President to impose sanctions on foreign vessels that the President determines knowingly transport LNG or certain other energy products originating in Russia, and on persons that provide services to such vessels. On October 16, 2026, the President issued Executive Order 14436, which waived the application of the sanctions, restrictions and duties provided for in the Graham Act. The waiver has no fixed expiration date, and it may be revoked or modified at any time. No sanctions have been imposed on us or the Vessels under the Graham Act. However, there can be no assurance that the waiver will remain in effect, or that sanctions will not be imposed under the Graham Act on us, the Vessels, the Charterer or our service providers, which could restrict or prevent the employment of the Vessels under the Yamal Charters and affect our access to insurance, financing and other services. General Our fleet consists of only six LNG carriers and we derive all our revenues from a limited number of charterers. For the nine-month period ended September 30, 2026, the Charterer accounted for approximately 34% of our total revenues, and the charter revenue expected to be generated by the Yamal Charters constituted approximately 56% of our estimated contract backlog. The loss of revenue under either or both of the Yamal Charters would have a material adverse effect on our business, results of operations, financial condition, cash flows and our ability to make distributions to our unitholders, and could result in an event of default under our debt agreements. Other than as described above in relation to the U.K. regulations, applicable U.S., U.K. and E.U. sanctions regimes that are in effect as of the date of this press release do not materially affect our business, operations or financial condition and, to our knowledge, our counterparties are currently performing their obligations under their respective time charters. We closely monitor the applicability of sanctions regulations on us and our counterparties, and the potential impact of economic sanctions on our existing commercial arrangements, including the Yamal Charters. The full impact of the commercial and economic consequences of the Russian war with Ukraine is uncertain at this time. The U.K., E.U. and U.S. measures described above or any further development in sanctions, or escalation of the Ukraine war and other geopolitical events and conflicts more generally may have a material adverse impact on our business, results of operations, financial condition, cash flows, our ability to make distributions to unitholders or our ability to comply with the covenants in our debt agreements. Sanctions have been expanded over time and may continue to evolve and could ultimately restrict or prevent the performance of certain contractual obligations under our charters. articles.body: Biofuel Bunker Snapshot: B30 premiums widen as conventional bunker prices drop in International Shipping News 23/11/2026 Europe Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO (POMEME) price has edged up $7/mt in the past week, while the Dutch port’s conventional VLSFO price has dropped $48/mt to $678/mt. This has widened Rotterdam’s B30-VLSFO price premium over conventional VLSFO by $55/mt to $194/mt. Rotterdam’s B30-LSMGO (POMEME) price has dropped $56/mt to $1,228/mt, while the port’s conventional LSMGO price has fallen a steeper $144/mt to $1,122/mt. This has widened the blend’s premium over conventional LSMGO by $88/mt to $106/mt. B100 has been priced at $1,235/mt in Rotterdam today, up $63/mt on the week. Prima Markets’ ARA UCOME and POMEME barge prices, both indicators of feedstock sourcing costs, have each dropped $72/mt in the past week, to $1,611/mt and $1,681/mt respectively. That leaves UCOME at a $70/mt discount to POMEME. Dutch suppliers can generate ZRE-A tickets for selling low-carbon fuels, which can be traded with other suppliers. The price of these tickets has dropped from €197.5/mtCO2e ($219/mtCO2e) last Thursday to €170/mtCO2e ($187/mtCO2e) on Thursday this week. These ZRE-A tickets help lower Rotterdam’s biofuel prices compared with other ports. Belgium has no such mechanism. Lower ZRE-A ticket prices could have supported Rotterdam’s B100 price. In neighbouring Antwerp, B100 (UCOME) has been priced at $1,901/mt today, down $31/mt on the week. This puts it at a $666/mt premium over Rotterdam. Belgium has no RED III mechanism, which is why the port’s price is considerably higher. In Portugal’s Aveiro, B30-LSMGO has been priced at $1,364/mt this week, down $73/mt on the week. B100 at the port has been priced at $1,581/mt, $12/mt lower than last week. Asia Singapore’s B30-VLSFO (UCOME) price has dropped $20/mt in the past week to $954/mt, while the port’s conventional VLSFO price has fallen a steeper $40/mt to $812/mt. This has widened Singapore’s B30-VLSFO price premium over conventional VLSFO by $20/mt to $142/mt. Prima Markets’ price assessment for China UCOME cargo, which is a key feedstock for Singapore’s B30-VLSFO blend, has held steady at $1,240/mt. Singapore’s bio-blended bunker sales fell sharply in October, decreasing by 33% to 54,000 mt, which was the lowest monthly volume since July. B100 has been priced at $1,354/mt in Singapore today, down $20/mt on the week. Hong Kong’s B30-VLSFO price has dropped $20/mt in the past week to $980/mt, while the port’s conventional VLSFO price has fallen $55/mt to $826/mt. This has widened its premium over conventional VLSFO by $35/mt to $154/mt. That leaves Hong Kong’s B30-VLSFO still at a $26/mt premium over Singapore’s B30-VLSFO. Hong Kong’s B30-HSFO has dropped $43/mt to $818/mt, a $79/mt premium over the port’s conventional HSFO price of $739/mt. In other biofuel bunker news, Kvasir Technologies and Crossbridge Energy have agreed to test co-processing Kvasir’s bio-oil, made from forestry and farm residues, at Crossbridge’s Fredericia refinery in Denmark to make greener ship fuel, with laboratory tests due this year and a full-scale trial planned for 2027. articles.body: Water levels on Rhine rise, providing relief to market participants in International Shipping News 23/11/2026 Water levels on the Rhine rose above 140 centimeters Nov. 20 and are forecast to exceed 250 cm over the weekend, providing relief to market participants after months of critical lows at Kaub, Germany, the shallowest part of the Middle Rhine. Levels at Kaub stood at 144 cm as of late afternoon Nov. 20, up from around 127 cm the previous day, according to the German water authority WSV. Levels were forecast to climb further to around 200 cm by the end of Nov. 21, following a few days of prolonged rain. The levels are expected to exceed 250 cm on Nov. 22, supporting greater barge activity, after record low levels had constrained transportation during the summer and most of autumn. Kaub water levels stood at 23 cm on average in September, at 19 cm in October and at 28 cm over the first half of November. The last time the Kaub water levels were above 150 cm was at the beginning of June. At levels below 150 cm, barges carrying more than 2,000 metric tons must reduce cargo loads to sail safely, prompting shipowners to impose surcharges to offset lost capacity. If river depth falls below 135 cm, barge loads are generally halved. Levels below 75 cm reduce loads to around 25% of capacity. If the levels are below 55 cm only around 16.6% of capacity is used. At 40 cm and below, barge traffic can stop completely, according to S&P Global Energy CERA analysts. Rising Rhine water levels helped conditions to normalize, with barge freight costs falling significantly over several days as loading conditions improved, a European-based market participant told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. Freight costs from Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp hub to Basel, Switzerland, were at €92.5/mt ($101.59/mt) on Nov. 20, down from €162.5/mt at the beginning of the week, Spotbarge data showed. ‘Fairly normal water territory’ While stocks remained very low and a backlog still needed to be cleared, the source said the Rhine was now in “fairly normal water territory.” At Maxau, levels above 400 cm still implied some loading restrictions, the source said, although sustained barge loadings of around 1,800-2,000 mt would represent much more normal operating conditions. A Germany-based diesel market participant said they booked the first fully laden barge down the Rhine in four months. The disruption had driven up freight costs per metric ton significantly and pushed German refiners to run at maximum capacity to compensate for the loss of inflows from the Amsterdam-Rotterdam-Antwerp hub, according to another participant. With ARA imports effectively curtailed, German refineries capitalized on elevated margins, according to market participants. Product from local refiners was actively displacing imports, with stocks being released into the market even in the absence of strong underlying demand. Consumption has been weighed down by a combination of factors: the ongoing transition toward electric vehicles and gasoline-powered cars, and a pullback in business and agricultural demand. Farmers were trying to purchase only the minimum volumes of fuel required during the agricultural season, holding back in anticipation of a decline in flat prices, one market participant noted. Rail options to expand A temporary tax relief measure on road fuels provided some demand support, but market participants flagged that the relief is due to expire at year-end, removing a key demand cushion heading into the winter months. Despite low stock levels, the market is not particularly concerned, given the balance struck between high domestic refinery output and subdued consumption, according to Platts sources. Platts assessed the European diesel benchmark ultra low sulfur diesel 10ppmS CIF Northwest Europe cargo price at $1,205.25/mt Nov. 19, below a peak of $1,642.25/mt Sept. 15. In contrast, the price averaged $714.72/mt in February before the Middle East war unfolded. The European benchmark physical FOB ARA 10ppm diesel barge crack was at $66.97/barrel on Nov. 19, its lowest point since Oct. 12. Planned refinery turnarounds in the first quarter could reduce domestic production capacity at the same time as scheduled lock maintenance on the Rhine limits barge movements, potentially constraining both supply and logistics simultaneously, market participants noted. Rail options in Germany, however, should expand in December, with the ongoing closure for refurbishment of the right-bank Middle Rhine Line, a key German freight route, scheduled to finish on Dec. 12. articles.body: Drewry: Intra Asia Container Index Keeps Grinding Higher in International Shipping News 23/11/2026 Drewry’s Intra-Asia Container Index (IACI) edged up $4 to $1,444 per 40ft container. IACI remains steady amid diverging regional trends • The Drewry Intra-Asia Container Index (IACI), a benchmark widely used by procurement teams, edged up $4 to $1,444 per 40ft container. Rates remained broadly stable, as easing pressure on the North Asian corridor was offset by rising tensions across Southeast Asian trade routes. • Spot rates from Greater China to Northeast, Southeast and South Asia recorded mixed performance this week. The Greater China–North Asia corridor exerted downwards pressure on the index as port congestion continued to ease. Rates to Busan declined 8% to $990 per 40ft container, while those to Kaohsiung fell 3% to $1,257 per 40ft container, as average vessel waiting times decreased three hours at Busan and four hours at Kaohsiung. In contrast, the Greater China–Southeast Asia corridor supported the index with rates to Manila rising 7% to $1,310 per 40ft container, whereas those to Laem Chabang increased 2% to $1,584 per 40ft container, as average vessel waiting times increased four hours and two hours, respectively. Congestion also intensified at major transhipment hubs, particularly Singapore, pushing Shanghai–Singapore rates up 1% to $2,064 per 40ft container. Meanwhile, Shanghai–Jebel Ali rates remained broadly stable at $8,149 per 40ft container, while rates from Shanghai to South Asia increased $151 to $3,141 per 40ft container. Drewry expects rates to decline over the coming weeks as additional capacity and improving port conditions exert downwards pressure on the market. • Spot rates across Southeast and Northeast Asian trade routes recorded an unusual mixed performance this week, with rates showing contrasting trends. Rates on Busan–Shanghai increased $14 to $203 per 40ft container, while those on Jawaharlal Nehru Port–Shanghai declined $6 to $52 per 40ft container. Meanwhile, OOCL is set to launch the FCS4 shuttle service in late November, connecting Chennai and Visakhapatnam with Port Klang. The service will enhance connectivity for Indian transhipment cargo and strengthen trade links between Malaysia and India’s east coast. It will complement the two intra-Asia services introduced by OOCL earlier this year from Jawaharlal Nehru Port and Mundra, further expanding connections to Southeast Asian markets. • The intra-Asia container freight market has remained resilient this year, with the index surging 117% YoY. Weather-related disruption remains a key risk for intra-Asia trade, as port closures and vessel delays could constrain capacity and exert further upwards pressure on freight rates. Meanwhile, escalating tensions in the Middle East have heightened market volatility, while elevated bunker costs continue to support rates. Drewry’s Intra-Asia Container Index (IACI) reports actual spot container freight rates for major intra-Asia trade routes. The Index, which will be updated weekly (from 02 Jan 26), consists of 18 route-specific indices representing individual shipping routes and a composite index. All indices are reported in USD per 40ft container. Finnish Border Guard/Handout via REUTERS HELSINKI, Nov 22 (Reuters) – A fire onboard a Russian cargo ship that was struck by drones in the Baltic Sea continued to burn through the night even as efforts were made to douse the flames, Finland’s coast guard said on Sunday. The Finnish military has said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was likely carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters where it remains at anchor. The 16 crew members were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship. Pictures and video released by the coast guard showed several vessels spraying the Sparta II with water cannons during the night in a bid to put out the flames and cool down containers stacked on its deck. Ukraine has sent waves of military drones towards Russia’s northwest coastal Leningrad region this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling onto NATO territory. The ship, bound for Russian exclave Kaliningrad, was damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland island, Finland’s Defence Forces have said, corroborating an account by Russian officials. The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, cannot be ruled out, Estonian Navy Commander Ivo Vark told public broadcaster ERR on Sunday. Finland’s military said last week it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks. The Sparta II is a 121-m (397-foot) Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned by Russian shipping company Oboronlogistika that left St Petersburg on Friday, according to LSEG data. The vessel is subject to US sanctions, according to the US Treasury Department. Oboronlogistika provides logistics services for the Russian Defence Ministry, according to the company’s website. articles.title: Russian Military-Linked Cargo Ship Burns After Suspected Drone Strike in Gulf of Finland
articles.summary: A Russian cargo ship linked to Moscow’s military logistics network caught fire after a drone strike in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday, drifting into Finnish territorial waters and triggering...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Flames and thick smoke rise from the Russian-flagged cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland on November 21, 2026, following a suspected drone attack. The vessel later drifted into Finnish territorial waters, prompting a response by Finnish authorities. A Russian cargo ship linked to Moscow’s military logistics network caught fire after a drone strike in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday, drifting into Finnish territorial waters and triggering an emergency maritime rescue operation. The Russian-flagged Sparta II , a sanctioned cargo vessel with a history of transporting military equipment, was struck in international waters west of Gogland Island, known in Finnish as Suursaari, according to Finland’s Ministry of Defence. Finnish military authorities detected the attack at approximately 8:40–8:50 a.m. local time, when the vessel was roughly 50 kilometers west of the island. The damaged ship subsequently lost maneuverability and drifted into Finnish territorial waters, where the Finnish Border Guard assumed responsibility for coordinating rescue operations. The incident took another turn shortly after midday when a Russian helicopter was suspected of entering Finnish airspace near Loviisa, reaching as far as 4.1 kilometers (2.5 miles) into Finnish territory. Finland’s Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen said the suspected airspace violation may have been connected to rescue or surveillance operations involving the damaged cargo ship. “The suspected airspace violation may be related to rescue or monitoring operations concerning the damaged cargo vessel in the Gulf of Finland,” Häkkänen said in a statement translated from Finnish. The Finnish Border Guard is investigating the incident, which occurred at approximately 12:34 p.m. local time. Fire Raises Fears of Explosions and Sinking The Sparta II remained ablaze Saturday afternoon, with Finnish authorities warning that the uncontrolled fire could lead to further explosions or even the loss of the vessel. The Finnish Border Guard said rescue vessels had reached the scene south of Loviisa, where authorities established a restricted area around the damaged ship. An official update issued at 2:58 p.m. local time said the crew had not been forced to abandon the vessel and that no environmental damage had been detected. Finnish authorities were preparing to assist with firefighting, evacuate personnel if necessary, and respond to any marine pollution. In a subsequent briefing reported by Yle, Finnish officials said the ship’s 16 crew members were evacuating into rescue craft. The vessel had anchored at approximately 3:45 p.m., and the anchor was holding. Russian rescue vessels were expected to arrive later Saturday. According to Finnish officials, Russia intended to tow Sparta II back into Russian waters once rescue operations were completed. The Finnish Border Guard emphasized that foreign vessels would require Finnish permission to participate in rescue operations within its area of responsibility. Sanctioned Vessel With Russian Military Connections The roll-on/roll-off Sparta II , IMO 9160994, is associated with Oboronlogistika, a Russian state-linked logistics company that provides maritime transportation services supporting the Russian Ministry of Defence. The vessel has previously been identified as part of Russia’s military logistics network, including operations involving the movement of military equipment between Russian ports and overseas locations. Sparta II was sanctioned by the United States in 2022 over its connections to Oboronlogistika and has been linked to shipments of military equipment from Syria to Russia. The ship has also operated cargo services connecting mainland Russia with its Baltic exclave of Kaliningrad, carrying vehicles, containers and other freight. Despite its military connections, Finnish authorities said they could not confirm whether the vessel was carrying weapons or military equipment when it was attacked. Finland Imposes Air and Maritime Restrictions The drone strike prompted Finland to reintroduce temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime activity in the eastern Gulf of Finland. The Ministry of Defence said the measures were intended to protect civilians and allow authorities to respond to any additional drone threats. Finland also notified its allies of the incident, underscoring the security implications of a military attack taking place near the territorial waters of a NATO member. Finnish authorities said they had received information about Ukrainian drone operations targeting Russia’s Leningrad region earlier Saturday and had taken precautions against drones potentially straying into Finnish territory. Although Finnish officials linked the attack on Sparta II to Ukrainian drones, there was no independently verified confirmation of responsibility from Kyiv in the official statements reviewed. Finland’s Defence Forces said the incident did not represent an immediate military threat to the country and that commercial shipping in the Baltic Sea had not been endangered. War Reaches Another Baltic Shipping Corridor The incident highlights the growing risks to commercial shipping as the war between Russia and Ukraine extends beyond the Black Sea. The Gulf of Finland is one of Russia’s most important maritime corridors, providing access to the Baltic Sea from St. Petersburg and the major oil and cargo terminals at Ust-Luga and Primorsk. It is also a heavily trafficked international shipping route bordered by NATO members Finland and Estonia. Unlike the Black Sea, where merchant vessels have repeatedly been caught up in military operations, the Gulf of Finland has remained a major commercial shipping corridor despite heightened tensions and security concerns since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The attack on Sparta II raises fresh questions about the vulnerability of Russian military-linked shipping in the Baltic and the potential consequences for neighboring countries when damaged vessels drift across maritime boundaries. It also illustrates the challenges facing coastal authorities when a military incident involving a sanctioned foreign vessel develops into a maritime rescue and potential pollution emergency. The Finnish Border Guard said the situation did not pose a danger to other maritime traffic, while rescue and firefighting operations continued in coordination with other authorities. The fate of Sparta II , including whether the damaged ship can be safely towed back to Russian waters, remains uncertain. REUTERS/Caroline Brehman Nov 21 (Reuters) – The Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) employers group at the Los Angeles and Long Beach ports said on Saturday it had reached a tentative agreement with the union for security guards, averting a strike that could have disrupted operations at the two busiest cargo shipping hubs in the US. The International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 represents 250 security officers, or watchmen, who account for a small fraction of the ports’ workforce, but their work is critical because they control access at terminal gates, conduct security patrols and report safety issues. PMA, which represents terminal owners, said the agreement reached on Saturday was subject to ratification by Local 26 members, and the current contract will be extended pending ratification. The union did not immediately respond to a request for comment sent outside regular business hours. The two sides resumed federally mediated negotiations on Friday, two days after the parties broke off talks , with the employers group reporting “little-to-no movement from the union on PMA’s proposals.” The PMA said at the time that its offer included a one-time bonus of $3,200 for each union member and a wage proposal that would raise average annual earnings for full-time watchmen from more than $170,000 to $198,000. The offer also called for maintaining fully employer-paid healthcare for active workers and retirees, valued at more than $62,000 each year, and increased pension benefits up to $93,200 a year for workers with the longest tenure. Talks between the terminal owners and the union have stretched on for more than a year. (Reporting by Akanksha Khushi in Bengaluru, Steve Gorman and Lisa Baertlein in Los Angeles. Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy Port of Long Beach More than 110 U.S. trade associations are urging waterfront employers and union leaders to reach a labor agreement and avert a potentially crippling strike at the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, with the latest contract extension set to expire just after midnight Saturday. The warning comes as the Pacific Maritime Association (PMA) and International Longshore and Warehouse Union (ILWU) Local 26 face a critical deadline following more than a year of negotiations over a contract covering approximately 250 port security workers. In a joint statement Friday, the associations called on both sides to remain at the bargaining table, negotiate in good faith and keep cargo moving through the nation’s busiest container port complex. “The Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach already face congestion from near-record import volumes,” the groups warned, adding that a work stoppage would jeopardize holiday shipments, disrupt manufacturing supply chains and restrict U.S. exports. The statement was backed by major organizations including the National Retail Federation, U.S. Chamber of Commerce, National Association of Manufacturers, American Trucking Associations and more than 100 other groups representing retailers, manufacturers, agricultural producers and logistics providers. The associations warned that a prolonged disruption could quickly spread beyond the waterfront, affecting trucking companies, railroads, warehouses and distribution networks nationwide. Container backlogs could take weeks or months to clear even after operations resume, they said. A Small Union With an Outsized Impact Although Local 26 represents only about 2% of the ILWU workforce at the two ports, its members perform security duties at terminals handling a substantial share of Southern California’s container traffic. According to PMA, the six container terminals covered by the dispute account for approximately 85% of cargo at Long Beach and 33% at Los Angeles. The larger concern is that thousands of longshore workers, marine clerks and foremen covered by separate labor agreements could honor Local 26 picket lines, effectively shutting down cargo operations at affected terminals. PMA warned Wednesday that negotiations held November 17 ended with little progress, while the union had already authorized a strike and indicated it was unwilling to extend the current agreement beyond 12:01 a.m. Pacific time Saturday. The two sides were scheduled to return to the negotiating table Friday in a final effort to avert a work stoppage. The more than 110 trade associations urged both parties to pursue a resolution that protects workers, employers and consumers rather than risk a disruption with nationwide economic consequences. articles.title: Iran War Oil Premium Evaporates as Global Crude Supplies Surge
articles.summary: The price of US sour oil has plunged, as a surge in crude supply from Venezuela, Canada and the Middle East gives refiners ample barrels to choose from.

Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche By Nathan Risser and Yongchang Chin (Bloomberg) –The price of US sour oil has plunged, as a surge in crude supply from Venezuela, Canada and the Middle East gives refiners ample barrels to choose from. US medium sour export grade Mars traded at a record premium to benchmark West Texas Intermediate futures in the early days of the Iran war. Buyers turned to the Gulf of Mexico variety, which is similar in quality to Middle Eastern crude, as the closure of the Strait of Hormuz disrupted supplies. Now, as oil markets begin to settle after a volatile year, Mars has fallen to a deep discount, making it cheaper for US refiners built to process heavier crude. Mars has dropped from a $10 premium to a $4 discount to WTI futures in less than a month. That’s the steepest discount since late September. Mars rallied to record premium of $17.50 at the peak of supply disruptions in March and April. At the start of the year, before the US and Israel launched their war in Iran in late February, the grade largely traded at a discount. Rising production of heavy-sour crude in Venezuela and Canada has pushed global prices lower in recent weeks. US refiners, major buyers of heavier oil along the Gulf Coast and in the Midwest, have benefited from increased supplies from Canada and Latin America. At the same time, higher shipping costs are weighing on prices at the barrel’s origin by making overseas sales more expensive. Flows from the Persian Gulf have also increased. Higher Middle Eastern flows, however, have reduced the incentive for Asian refiners to take advantage of falling Mars prices, with the US grade still uneconomical to import, according to traders familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named because they aren’t authorized to speak to the media. On a delivered basis to Northeast Asia, Mars for February was priced at a premium of about $12 to $13 a barrel to the Dubai benchmark — around $10 more expensive than similar quality oil from Saudi Arabia, they said. At least one other seller of Middle Eastern crude has also slashed offer prices, they added. “Incremental supply looks to be dominated by heavier and more sour barrels, especially out of Canada, Venezuela, and the Middle East,” Valero’s head of crude supply Randy Hawkins said in an October earnings call. It’s a “race to the bottom” Phillips 66’s executive vice president of marketing and commercial Brian Mandell said on a call with analysts the same month. In Canada, the pipeline that takes oil sands crude from inland fields to export markets on the West Coast is operating at a record 960,000 barrels a day this month, 8% above its stated capacity. Oil will also be shipped on 34 vessels out of the Westridge terminal near Vancouver in November, up from 31 in October. While cheaper heavy crude is a boon to refiners who are already making record profits from the Iran war’s disruptions to global fuel markets, it is coming at a cost to heavy oil producers. “We’re basically going to have to be a price taker,” oil driller Sable Offshore Corp. chief executive office Jim Flores said earlier this month. Sable pumps heavy oil off the coast of California. For now, US crude exports of both heavy and light grades continue at historically elevated levels. US crude exports averaged 4 million barrels a day over the past four weeks, below the weekly record of more than 6 million set in April but well above the 3 million average since the US lifted its crude-export ban in 2015. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. articles.body: Tanker On Fire After Struck By Projectile Near Strait of Hormuz Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 © Adobe Stock/IbrahimAlkan A tanker caught fire after being struck by an unknown projectile while sailing outbound through the Strait of Hormuz, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Friday. The British navy-affiliated agency UKMTO said that the incident occurred 8 nautical miles north of the Omani town of Khasab, adding that no casualties or environmental impact were reported. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said shortly afterwards that an oil tanker had caught fire after hitting a mine while attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz near Khasab, Iranian state media reported. Khasab lies on Oman's Musandam Peninsula at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway that carried nearly one-fifth of global crude oil supplies before the US-Israeli conflict with Iran. Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has been disrupted since Iran moved to close the waterway following the eruption of the conflict on February 28. (Reuters)

articles.title: Oil Prices Drop for Third Week Straight
articles.summary: Oil prices fell on Friday and were set for a weekly decline on strong exports from the Middle East despite Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.Brent crude futures were down 67 cents, or 0.7%, at $91.31 a barrel at 1414 GMT.
articles.body: Oil Prices Drop for Third Week Straight Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Zulfugar Karimov Oil prices fell on Friday and were set for a weekly decline on strong exports from the Middle East despite Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude futures were down 67 cents, or 0.7%, at $91.31 a barrel at 1414 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate futures for December were down 36 cents, or 0.4%, at $82.85 a barrel, while the more active January contract was down 19 cents, or 0.2%, at $82.85. Brent is on track for a near 5% decline for the week and the December WTI contract for a 6.5% weekly drop as expectations of a supply surplus grew because crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels. This would be the benchmarks' third straight week of decline. "This week we keep having relatively strong export flows out of the Middle East. There is also a narrative ongoing that as long as people are talking, maybe there's a deal in the making," said Aldo Spanjer, commodity strategist at BNP Paribas. "The prices are correct if you believe that this geopolitical risk doesn't come back. I'm not in that camp who thinks this is done ... I probably see a rebound," he said. On Friday, the Iran-aligned Houthi movement warned workers and people near Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports to evacuate immediately and urged shipping companies to remove vessels, saying they would target Saudi ports in Jeddah and the Red Sea if a Saudi-led coalition strikes Yemen's Hodeidah port. The Houthis fired missiles at Riyadh on Thursday. Two oil tankers also hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz and "are burning," Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a statement carried by state media on Thursday. Iran's intensifying attacks on tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz, "running at roughly one incident per day in November," still add a meaningful geopolitical risk premium to the market, according to UOB Group analysts in a client note. OPEC+ ministers will hold a series of meetings on November 29 to decide their 2027 output policy. The group comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia. The Middle East conflict has caused the biggest disruption ever to global oil and gas trade and could cut world oil demand by more than 4% by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response, the International Energy Agency said on Thursday. However, some analysts expect softness in the broader equities markets to weigh on oil prices, as Asian shares fell on Friday — heading for their worst week since 2020. "Supply disruptions remain a risk, but near-term demand concerns tied to the AI trade unwind and broader risk-off sentiment are weighing on prices," said Saxo analysts in a note. In Russia, crude oil output could fall again as Ukrainian attacks on refineries and export infrastructure intensify, analysts and traders say. Ukrainian drone a ttacks have cut Russian oil refineries' combined crude processing volumes by 45% since late October, Reuters reported on Wednesday. (Reuters)

articles.title: US Treasury Urges Singapore, Malaysia of Compliance With Iran Sanctions
articles.summary: US Treasury Department officials met with government authorities in Singapore and Malaysia this week, including regulators and national security bodies, to warn of potential risks they could face if they do not comply with US sanctions on Iran.Washington is urging the countries…
articles.body: US Treasury Urges Singapore, Malaysia of Compliance With Iran Sanctions Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 © Adobe Stock/christianthiel.net US Treasury Department officials met with government authorities in Singapore and Malaysia this week, including regulators and national security bodies, to warn of potential risks they could face if they do not comply with US sanctions on Iran. Washington is urging the countries, as well as law firms and banks operating there, to stay alert for Iranian front companies, as it steps up efforts to enforce sanctions in Asia and bring about a speedy end to the conflict in the Middle East. The US is urging additional scrutiny on "high-risk" sectors such as maritime transport, aviation services and procurement networks, "to make sure they're not fronting for Iran," said a Treasury Department official. "We want it to be understood too, that we're going to target these lifelines, and it's not going to be a negotiation when we find a lifeline that needs to be targeted," the official said. Since the US and Israel commenced strikes on Iran in February, the US has intensified actions to throttle Tehran's business interests overseas. In August, President Donald Trump's administration launched Operation Economic Outcast, resulting in a barrage of sanctions against targets spanning Canadian digital currency platforms to a major Russian banking group. OIL ON WATER For years, tankers have regularly made stops in the waters around Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia to make ship-to-ship transfers of Iranian oil that help obscure its origin. Last year, Malaysian authorities said they would more tightly enforce rules around these transfers and in February seized two tankers and their cargoes. Since April, the US Navy has imposed a blockade on shipping reaching Iran through the Strait of Hormuz, and this month has cracked down on movement over Iran's land borders and through the Caspian Sea. In July, the Treasury Department sanctioned dozens of individuals, vessels and companies based in Singapore, Hong Kong, the UAE, the Marshall Islands and St Kitts and Nevis linked to Iranian oil magnate Mohammad Hossein Shamkhani. These efforts were starting to disrupt Iran's source of revenue, the US official said, citing data showing that the country is currently undergoing the worst GDP contraction in four decades and the highest rate of inflation since World War II. IRANIAN AIRLINES However, the official said there was still work to be done. "There's an Iranian airline that flies to Malaysia, or has, recently, so we raised this," the US official said, without naming the carrier. Using public flight records, Reuters identified a regularly scheduled flight between Tehran and Kuala Lumpur operated by Iran Airtour, which flew as recently as November 14. A scheduled flight on November 17 did not depart, the records also show. Iran Airtour did not respond to an emailed request for comment sent outside of business hours on Friday. Most Iranian airlines largely stopped flying to Malaysia in 2022 due to US sanctions on refuelling Iranian planes. However, Iran Airtour, a privately owned airline, resumed flights to Malaysia in November 2025, according to Iranian media. On September 8, the US imposed sanctions on dozens of companies in the UAE, Britain, Malaysia, Turkey and Kazakhstan it said were supporting Iran's aviation sector to move weapons, personnel and illicit cargo. The following day, Iran Air officials met with Malaysia's ambassador to Iran to discuss resuming direct flights between Iran and Kuala Lumpur. 'DOING OUR PART' Both Malaysia and Singapore implement UN Security Council sanctions on Iran. Singapore's government said in a statement it "is firmly committed to doing our part" and "preventing bad actors from abusing our corporate vehicles," citing its efforts to strengthen vigilance in the maritime and financial industries this year. The Malaysian government did not respond to requests for comment. (Reuters)

articles.title: Saudi Forces Strike Hodeidah Port as Houthis Warn Airlines Away From Airspace
articles.summary: The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said it had struck the Red Sea port of Hodeidah to destroy Houthi capabilities on Friday, as the militants warned airlines to avoid Saudi airspace, pledging new air strikes within hours.The developments…
articles.body: Saudi Forces Strike Hodeidah Port as Houthis Warn Airlines Away From Airspace Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 © AU USAnakul / Adobe Stock The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said it had struck the Red Sea port of Hodeidah to destroy Houthi capabilities on Friday, as the militants warned airlines to avoid Saudi airspace, pledging new air strikes within hours. The developments, a day after the group struck the tallest skyscraper in Riyadh, signalled a worsening of a conflict that has brought a humanitarian crisis to Yemen and severe disruption to Saudi Arabia, in parallel with the US-led war against Iran. Hodeidah is the main port bringing food and other supplies into Houthi-controlled northern Yemen. The coalition had earlier warned civilians to evacuate the area. The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed operational capabilities at the port that were used in smuggling operations and the transport of weapons and ballistic missiles. The port remains fully operational and the flow of goods will continue, according to Yemen’s Information Minister. HOUTHIS TELL SHIPPING COMPANIES TO EVACUATE FROM SAUDI PORTS There was no immediate comment from the Houthis, who had earlier said they would hit Red Sea ports if the Saudis carried out their own threat to strike the Yemeni port. "We warn all employees, workers, and those in the vicinity of (Saudi Arabia's Red Sea) ports to evacuate them immediately and stay away. We also urge all shipping companies to immediately evacuate their ships from these ports," Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement. Airlines should avoid Saudi airspace "because it will be the scene of our operations in the coming hours," Saree said, making an exception for airspace near the Muslim holy cities of Mecca and Medina. He also said the group would target a power station at Shuqaiq in southern Saudi Arabia. The Saudi-led coalition also said it carried out an operation in Yemen's capital Sanaa targeting ballistic missile and drone capabilities and that operations in Saada and Taiz were ongoing. Since fighting resumed in Yemen in July in parallel with the wider Iran war, the Houthis have rapidly advanced in Yemen, seizing territory from Yemen's internationally recognised government and its allies, who are backed by Saudi Arabia. The Saudis have carried out air strikes on Yemen in support of their allies on the ground, while the Houthis have struck Saudi oil targets, airports and office towers. Deadly strikes on Riyadh's main airport last month led to the cancellation of most international flights, and Saudi Arabia has postponed or cancelled high-profile global events including soccer's AFC Asian Cup. Saudi Arabia, a close ally of the United States, has been backing Yemen's internationally recognised government for more than a decade in a war that was fought to a stalemate in 2022 but reignited in July this year. The Houthis have seized Yemen's Red Sea coast and forced the Saudi-backed forces aligned with the government to retreat over the weekend to defend their temporary capital in the southern port of Aden. (Reuters)

REUTERS/Stringer Another tanker was struck by a projectile and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday, extending a wave of attacks on commercial shipping that has pushed maritime security incidents to their highest weekly level since mid-October. The latest incident occurred at approximately 1500 UTC, eight nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman, according to UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) Warning 214-26 . The tanker was transiting outbound through the strategic waterway when an unknown projectile struck its port bow, sparking a fire onboard. The vessel’s company security officer reported no casualties or environmental impact. Authorities are investigating. The attack comes amid a sharp escalation in threats to merchant shipping across the Middle East and Black Sea. According to maritime security analyst Martin Kelly of Orbital Risk Intelligence, shipping experienced 15 attacks and piracy-related incidents over the past seven days, a 50% increase from the previous week and the highest weekly total since mid-October. In the Persian Gulf, Strait of Hormuz and Gulf of Oman, Kelly recorded seven strikes involving six vessels. Four tankers were hit within 13 nautical miles of Khasab over three days, including the LPG tanker TARA GAS , which was attacked twice. The violence has left two seafarers missing and 13 injured, according to Kelly’s assessment. Among the most serious incidents was the November 17 attack on the tanker NAVIG8 MESSI , which suffered a fire after being struck 13 nautical miles north of Khasab. ADNOC confirmed that one crew member was missing and 11 others were injured. The remaining crew were evacuated and the vessel was reported under tow. The TARA GAS , meanwhile, was disabled by a projectile strike on November 16 before being hit again the following day, resulting in another fire and the vessel being abandoned. The pattern points to an increasingly dangerous concentration of attacks along the southern shipping lanes off Oman’s Musandam Peninsula, particularly against tankers attempting to leave the Persian Gulf. The deteriorating security situation is taking a continued toll on commercial traffic. In its weekly maritime security overview published Friday , UKMTO reported 115 outbound and 148 inbound transits over the preceding seven days, down from 139 outbound and 169 inbound crossings the previous week. Combined traffic remains approximately 65% below pre-conflict levels. UKMTO recorded six verified attacks across the Strait of Hormuz and Persian Gulf during its latest reporting period, which covered incidents through November 18. Four occurred in the Strait itself and two in the wider Persian Gulf. Two vessels required assistance, while the outcomes of four others remained unknown. The agency cautioned that its figures do not capture every incident, as some reports cannot be independently verified. Since the U.S.-Iran ceasefire agreement expired on August 17, UKMTO has recorded six total vessel losses, while 22 vessels required assistance and 31 were confirmed to have continued their voyages. The Joint Maritime Information Center (JMIC) continues to assess the threat to commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz as SEVERE , warning that further deliberate attacks are highly likely. The surge in maritime violence extends well beyond the Middle East. Six commercial vessels were struck in the western Black Sea over the past week, according to Kelly, including two ships that sank in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone on consecutive days. The general cargo ship BETUL 8 sank on November 16, followed by the LPG tanker GAS HUSKY on November 17. All 31 seafarers aboard the two vessels were rescued. Maritime security firm Ambrey separately confirmed reports of six vessels struck since November 13, including four attacked near the Sulina anchorage in Romanian waters and two in Bulgarian waters. Ambrey assessed the attacks as part of an escalating Russian campaign involving unmanned aerial and surface vessels. The incidents have raised growing concerns about the safety of commercial shipping in waters adjacent to NATO member states Romania and Bulgaria. Piracy-related activity has also increased in the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean. During the week, a tanker reported being approached by an armed skiff carrying a ladder approximately 430 nautical miles east of Socotra, Yemen. In another incident off Al Mukalla, armed guards aboard a cargo vessel fired a warning shot to repel an attempted boarding. A further incident was reported Friday, when six armed men aboard a skiff fired four shots at an eastbound bulk carrier approximately 95 nautical miles southwest of Al Mukalla. The ship’s security team returned warning shots, forcing the attackers to retreat. No injuries or damage were reported. The incidents underscore the growing range of threats facing merchant vessels, from projectile and drone attacks in active conflict zones to renewed piracy activity along established trading routes. With attacks concentrated around the Strait of Hormuz and the western Black Sea, maritime security analysts warn that the coming week could bring further strikes against commercial vessels. November 20, 2026 © Dongara Marine The Cook Labor Government is investing $13.4 million in two new vessels to strengthen fisheries compliance and protect the Kimberley's valuable marine resources. A new nine-meter amphibious vessel is now operating out of Broome, undertaking patrols across the Buccaneer Archipelago Marine Park. The vessel was built by global business Sealegs who specialize in manufacturing the versatile craft. The vessel's ability to travel on both land and water will allow Fisheries and Marine Officers to access remote locations where extreme tidal conditions and limited boat ramp infrastructure can make launching traditional vessels difficult. The vessel will support joint patrols with local Aboriginal ranger groups, strengthening partnerships and supporting the shared management of the culturally significant region. The larger 22-meter patrol vessel will also be based in Broome, supporting commercial and recreational fisheries compliance and marine park management across northern waters. Expected to be delivered in October 2028, the new vessel will be built by Dongara Marine, providing another boost to Western Australia's marine manufacturing industry. The Geraldton business also delivered the new PV Equinox earlier this year, replacing the ageing PV Walcott and strengthening the State's fisheries patrol capabilities across the Kimberley.

articles.body: Hatenboer-Water Breaks Ground on New Headquarters in Schiedam Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 © Hatenboer-Water Hatenboer-Water has started building a new headquarters in Schiedam, driving the first foundation pile on Thursday after early demolition work. Due to finish in the third quarter of 2027, the new building project adds manufacturing space and twice the company's current testing capacity as orders grow across shipping and offshore energy. Hatenboer-Water's existing premises in Schiedam have reached their limit. Rebuilding on site upgrades its engineering workshops and manufacturing facilities and keeps the business inside the Port of Rotterdam maritime cluster. Schiedam's focus on maritime manufacturing puts the company close to European shipbuilders, engineering firms and offshore service providers. The site also serves as the main hub for regional offices in Aberdeen, Dubai, Houston, Singapore and Hamburg. Doubling production and testing capacity means Hatenboer-Water can build more systems and run several demanding tests simultaneously, cutting waiting times and speeding up delivery. Inside, the building includes new production equipment, a better layout for moving materials, shared meeting spaces for visiting clients, and upgraded IT infrastructure and access controls. Separate, fully secured office zones with restricted access will let teams work on confidential projects. Designed as an all-electric, fully insulated building, it will also operate without natural gas. Daily operations will not stop during construction. Using a phased 'chessboard' plan, the existing building will stay in use while the first new sections are built. Staff and equipment will move across step by step as each part finishes, keeping production and support running as normal through 2027.

articles.summary: Etu Energias has strengthened its position in Angola’s offshore energy industry with the acquisition of Azule Energy’s interests in two blocks.
articles.body: Business & Finance November 20, 2026 · 5 minutes ago Azule Energy wraps up divestment of two Angolan offshore blocks Etu Energias has strengthened its position in Angola’s offshore energy industry with the acquisition of Azule Energy’s interests in two blocks. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Illustration Source: Azule Energy As part of its optimization strategy, Azule Energy, a joint venture between two energy majors, Italy’s Eni and the UK’s BP, has finished the divestment of its participating interests in two blocks in the Lower Congo Basin, off the coast of Angola. Azule Energy has completed the sale of its participating interests in blocks 14 and 14K offshore Angola to Etu Energias. The transaction comprises 20% participating interest in Block 14 and 10% participating interest in Block 14K, with the completion following the fulfilment of the applicable conditions and receipt of the required approvals. The company explains that this transaction supports the continued optimization of its portfolio and focus on strategic priorities, while reinforcing its long-term commitment to the country and its energy sector. Rand Merchant Bank (RMB), a division of FirstRand Bank, served as the sole financial advisor to Azule Energy on the transaction. " The completion of this transaction is another important step in the continued optimisation of Azule Energy’s portfolio. It enables us to focus our investment and capabilities on our strategic priorities while maintaining our long-term commitment to Angola and its energy sector. We would like to thank our partners, RMB, the relevant authorities and all those involved in supporting a safe and orderly transition. " — Joe Murphy Chief Executive Officer of Azule Energy Azule Energy emphasizes that it remains firmly committed to Angola and will continue investing in the development of the country’s energy resources, supporting energy security, economic development, and a more sustainable energy future. " We extend our sincere congratulations to our partner Etu Energias on completing this transaction, which materially increases their participating interest in these assets and further cements their position as Angola’s leading private E&P company. For Chariot, completion delivers a strategic foothold in a prolific hydrocarbon province and exposure to cashflows from long-term oil production with material undeveloped upside potential, which we look forward to reporting on next year. This first acquisition has already led to a second transaction on the same asset, which on completion, will double our economic exposure in Angola, and we look forward to continuing to work closely with Etu Energias and Shell Trading on further opportunities. " — Adonis Pouroulis CEO of Chariot While Block 14 is a mid to late-life producing asset located within the Cabinda province offshore Angola, Block 14K is an adjacent unitised area which crosses the Angolan and Republic of Congo maritime border and ties back to Block 14. The fields on Block 14 have cumulatively produced over 900 million bbls of high-quality crude since first oil in 1999 and current production is approximately 40,000 bopd. Gross producing reserves from the assets are estimated to be 93 million bbls as of January 1, 2026, and there are material upsides on Block 14, notably further development of the PKBB discovery , as well as additional neighbouring discoveries that can utilise existing production and processing infrastructure. articles.body: Vice Adm. Burdian appointed as DHS Joint Task Force-Maritime Director Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 Vice Adm. Jo‑Ann Burdian. Image courtesy USCG Vice Adm. Jo‑Ann Burdian was presidentially appointed as the director, Department of Homeland Security Joint Task Force–Maritime (JTF-M), effective Nov. 10, 2026. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin nominated Burdian as director of JTF-M, in accordance with 6 U.S.C. § 348(b)(3)(A), to ensure the critical, continued role of JTF-M in synchronizing multi-agency maritime operations and securing the nation’s maritime borders. “Vice Admiral Burdian’s appointment as the JTF-M director marks a pivotal moment for our collective maritime defense," said Mullin. "Her unmatched operational expertise is critical as JTF-M continues to dismantle illicit networks, prevent hostile exploitation of our maritime borders, and leverage the MOC-P construct to achieve departmental unity of effort and drive nationwide success." JTF-M synchronizes DHS component operations, intelligence, and investigations across the maritime domain to secure U.S. borders, prevent and respond to homeland security crises and facilitate regionally based joint operations. As the DHS Maritime Operations Coordination Plan (MOC-P) program office, JTF-M enhances coordination among DHS components, eliminating redundancy and increasing effectiveness through 35 Regional Coordinating Mechanisms (ReCoMs). These ReCoMs execute DHS missions at every major U.S. port, along all U.S. coastlines and approaches to maritime borders of the U.S. and its territories. The ReCoMs help prevent terrorist, criminal, and hostile activities and dismantle illicit networks attempting to exploit the maritime domain and reduce vulnerabilities while safeguarding legal trade and travel. "I am honored to lead the dedicated staff of Joint Task Force-Maritime as we strengthen our borders and streamline interagency response," said Burdian. "Through our 35 ReCoMs and strong partnerships with the Department of War, we will continue to safeguard legal trade and travel while remaining an impenetrable barrier against cross-border smuggling, illegal immigration and illicit trafficking." Burdian also serves as commander, Coast Guard Atlantic Area and commander, Coast Guard Defense Force East, providing Coast Guard forces and operations across all mission areas from the Arctic Ocean to the Arabian Gulf in support of the DoW and combatant commanders for national defense missions.

articles.title: Energy-Saving System for Marine Generators Touts 10% Fuel Savings
articles.summary: NYK Line, MTI Co., Oshima Shipbuilding, Terasaki Electric and Daihatsu Infinearth have verified the energy-saving performance and operational safety of the Hz Controller System, an energy-saving system for marine generators developed through joint testing.
articles.body: Energy-Saving System for Marine Generators Touts 10% Fuel Savings Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 20, 2026 Copyright Xavier MARCHANT/AdobeStock NYK Line, MTI Co., Oshima Shipbuilding, Terasaki Electric and Daihatsu Infinearth have verified the energy-saving performance and operational safety of the Hz Controller System, an energy-saving system for marine generators developed through joint testing. General sales of the system will now begin. Building on their joint research, the five companies will expand deployment beyond NYK-operated vessels, promoting installation on newbuildings and retrofitting on existing ships owned by other shipowners. The System reduces power consumption and generator fuel consumption by lowering the generator frequency while maintaining the performance required by onboard equipment. This is possible because onboard equipment such as pumps and motors that operate in conjunction with the power supply frequency is designed to deliver the required performance even under anticipated severe conditions and may therefore have excess capacity during normal navigation. Specifically, the System switches between the regular frequency and a lower energy-saving frequency according to shipboard conditions within the range specified by ship classification rules. It utilizes generator frequency control technology (Patent Number JP6238600) that is jointly patented by NYK and Tsuneishi Shipbuilding. Demonstration tests confirmed an approximately 10% reduction in generator fuel consumption compared with operation at the regular frequency. Subsequent verification on an increasing number of vessels equipped with the system confirmed a similar reduction. For general sales, Terasaki Electric will be responsible for the design and supply of the System, while Daihatsu Infinearth will expand its lineup of generator engines compatible with the System.

articles.title: 1 MW floating wave energy converter gets green light for test site deployment
articles.summary: WEDUSEA, a €19.6 million collaborative project bringing together 14 European partners, has secured a marine license that allows the installation...
articles.body: Tidal & Wave Energy November 20, 2026 · 1 minute ago 1 MW floating wave energy converter gets green light for test site deployment NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email EMEC WEDUSEA, a €19.6 million collaborative project bringing together 14 European partners, has secured a marine license that allows the installation of a 1 MW OE Buoy floating wave energy converter and associated moorings at the European Marine Energy Centre's (EMEC) test site in Orkney. Co-funded by the EU Horizon Europe Programme and Innovate UK, WEDUSEA, which brings together 14 partners from industry and academia across Ireland, the UK, France, Germany and Spain, aims to create a step change for the wave energy industry and support its progression towards commercialization. The marine license granted by the Marine Directorate, previously Marine Scotland, allows the 1 MW-rated, unmanned floating oscillating water column device, developed by OceanEnergy, to be deployed at EMEC. Its only moving part, the turbine rotor, sits on deck above the waves, while all electrical equipment is housed below deck in a sealed machine room. As waves cause air trapped within the OE Buoy hull to oscillate, the airflow drives the turbine to generate electricity. This electricity will be exported to the grid via an underwater umbilical and export cable, EMEC explained. The OE Buoy and its mooring system will be installed at Berth 5 at the Billia Croo wave energy test site. Furthermore, EMEC has developed an extensive environmental monitoring plan for the deployment, which will monitor the habitat above and below the water’s surface in the vicinity of the OE Buoy. The monitoring program will begin before installation to establish a baseline of benthic and pelagic activity in the deployment area, helping to build understanding of the marine environment before, during and following deployment.
